l: India
India, officially the Republic of India, is a country in <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color>. It is the world's seventh-largest country by area and the
largest by population. Bounded by the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color> on the south, the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Sea</color> on the southwest, and the <color=#3366CC>Bay of</color>

<color=#3366CC>Bengal</color> on the southeast, it shares land borders with <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> to the west; <color=#3366CC>China</color>, <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Bhutan</color> to the north; and
<color=#3366CC>Bangladesh</color> and <color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color> to the east. In the Indian Ocean, India is near <color=#3366CC>Sri Lanka</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Maldives</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Modern humans</color> arrived on the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> from <color=#3366CC>Africa</color> by 55,000 years ago. Their long, isolated occupation as
hunter-gatherers made the region highly diverse. <color=#3366CC>Settled life</color> emerged on the western margins of the <color=#3366CC>Indus</color> <color=#3366CC>basin</color> 9,000
years ago, evolving into the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley Civilisation</color> by the third millennium BCE. By, an <color=#3366CC>archaic form</color> of <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color> had

<color=#3366CC>diffused</color> into India from the northwest, <color=#3366CC>its hymns</color> recording the <color=#3366CC>early dawnings</color> of <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>. India's pre-existing
<color=#3366CC>Dravidian languages</color> were supplanted in the northern regions. By, social differentiation by <color=#3366CC>caste</color> had consolidated within
Hinduism. Contemporarily, Buddhism and <color=#3366CC>Jainism</color> had arisen, proclaiming <color=#3366CC>social orders</color> unlinked to <color=#3366CC>heredity</color>. The
emergence of the loose-knit <color=#3366CC>Maurya</color> and <color=#3366CC>Gupta Empires</color>, gave rise to wide-ranging cultural and scientific creativity, but
their eras also witnessed a steady erosion of women's rights, and, by the end, the rigid institutionalisation of
untouchability. Concurrently accross the first millennium CE, the <color=#3366CC>Middle kingdoms</color> of <color=#3366CC>South India</color> transmitted Dravidian
language scripts and cultures to <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>. Well before the millennium's end, Judaism, Christianity, Islam and
Zoroastrianism had become established on India's southern and western coasts.
Early in the 2nd millennium, Muslim armies from <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> intermittently overran India's northern plaints, eventually
establishing the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color>, and drawing India into the <color=#3366CC>cosmopolitan networks of medieval Islam</color>. The
<color=#3366CC>Vijayanagara Empire</color> created a long-lasting composite South Indian culture. <color=#3366CC>Sikhism</color> emerged in the <color=#3366CC>Punjab</color>, rejecting
institutionalised religion. The <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> ushered in two centuries of economic expansion and relative peace,
leaving a rich architectural legacy. Gradually expanding rule of the British East India Company turned India into a
colonial economy but consolidated its <color=#3366CC>sovereignty</color>. <color=#3366CC>British Crown rule</color> began in 1858. The rights promised to Indians
were granted slowly, but <color=#3366CC>technological changes</color> were introduced, and modern education and the public life took root. <color=#3366CC>A</color>
<color=#3366CC>nationalist movement</color> emerged in India, the first in the non-European <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color>. Noted for nonviolent resistance
after 1920, it became the primary factor in ending British rule. In 1947, the British Indian Empire was <color=#3366CC>partitioned</color> into
two independent dominions, a Hindu-majority dominion of India and a Muslim-majority dominion of Pakistan. A
large-scale loss of life and an unprecedented migration accompanied the partition.
Since 1950, India has been a federal republic, governed through a democratic <color=#3366CC>parliamentary system</color>. It is a pluralistic,
<color=#3366CC>multilingual</color> and <color=#3366CC>multi-ethnic society</color>. India's population grew from 361 million in 1951 to over 1.4 billion in 2023. Its
fast-growing <color=#3366CC>economy</color> is a hub for information technology, with an expanding middle class. India has reduced poverty,
though alongside increasing economic inequality. It is a nuclear-weapon state, with high military expenditure, and holds
unresolved mid-20th-century disputes over <color=#3366CC>Kashmir</color> with its neighbours, Pakistan and China. Socio-economic
challenges include gender inequality, child malnutrition, and rising air pollution. India's megadiverse land features four
biodiversity hotspots. Its wildlife is supported in protected habitats and traditionally viewed with <color=#3366CC>cultural</color> tolerance.
Etymology
According to the <color=#3366CC>Oxford English Dictionary</color>, the English proper noun "India" derives most immediately from the
<color=#3366CC>Classical Latin</color> India, a reference to a loosely-defined historical region of Asia stretching from <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color> to the borders

of China. Further <color=#3366CC>etymons</color> are: <color=#3366CC>Hellenistic Greek</color> India; <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greek</color> Indos, or the River <color=#3366CC>Indus</color>; Achaemenian Old
Persian <color=#3366CC>Hindu</color> (an eastern province of the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Empire</color>); and <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color> Sindhu, or "river," but specifically the
Indus river, and by extension its well-settled basin. The <color=#3366CC>Ancient Greeks</color> referred to South Asians as Indoi, 'the people of
the Indus'.
The term Bharat (Bhārat), mentioned in both Indian epic poetry and the <color=#3366CC>Constitution of India</color>, is used in its variations by
many Indian languages. A modern rendering of the historical name Bharatavarsha, which applied originally to <color=#3366CC>North</color>
<color=#3366CC>India</color>, Bharat gained increased currency from the mid-19th century as a native name for India.
Hindustan is a Middle Persian name for India that became popular by the 13th century, and was used widely since the
era of the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color>. The meaning of Hindustan has varied, referring to a region encompassing the northern
<color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> (present-day northern India and <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>) or to India in its near entirety.
History
Ancient India
Based on coalescence of <color=#3366CC>Mitochondrial DNA</color> and Y Chromosome data, it is thought that the earliest extant lineages of
anatomically modern humans or <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color> on the Indian subcontinent had reached there from Africa between
80,000 and 50,000 years ago, and with high likelihood by 55,000 years ago. Their long occupation, initially in varying
forms of isolation as hunter-gatherers, has made the region highly diverse, second only to Africa in human <color=#3366CC>genetic</color>
<color=#3366CC>diversity</color>. However, the earliest known modern human fossils in South Asia date to about 30,000 years ago. Evidence

for the <color=#3366CC>neolithic period</color> in the western margins of the <color=#3366CC>Indus</color> <color=#3366CC>river basin</color>, at Mehrgarh in <color=#3366CC>Balochistan, Pakistan</color>, dates to
after. Domestication of grain-producing plants (including <color=#3366CC>barley</color>) and animals (including <color=#3366CC>humped zebu</color> cattle) occurred
here. These cultures gradually evolved into the <color=#3366CC>Indus Valley Civilisation</color>, which flourished during in Pakistan and
western India. Centred around cities such as <color=#3366CC>Mohenjo-daro</color>, <color=#3366CC>Harappa</color>, Dholavira, Ganweriwala, and Rakhigarhi, its
characteristic features included standardised weights, steatite <color=#3366CC>seals</color>, a written script, urban planning, public works, and
arts and crafts including pottery styles, terracotta human figures and animal statuettes. Networks of towns and villages
grew around the cities in a new <color=#3366CC>agro</color>-<color=#3366CC>pastoral</color> economy.

Between and, an <color=#3366CC>archaic form</color> of <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color>, an <color=#3366CC>Indo-European language</color>, <color=#3366CC>diffused</color> into India from the northwest. Its
evidence today is found in the <color=#3366CC>Rig Veda</color>—the oldest <color=#3366CC>scripture</color> associated with what later became <color=#3366CC>Hinduism</color>—which was
composed by <color=#3366CC>Indo-Aryan</color>-speaking tribes migrating east from what is today northern <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color> and across the
<color=#3366CC>Punjab region</color>. The settling of the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> <color=#3366CC>river plain</color> took place during the next millennium, when large swathes of the
river system's adjoining regions were deforested, at times by setting fires, or later by employing iron implements, and
prepared for agriculture. The settlement may have involved driving the preexisting people out or enslaving them. The
<color=#3366CC>Dravidian languages</color> of India were supplanted in the north, creating a broad <color=#3366CC>language family</color>-divide, with the Indo-Aryan
languages being spoken mainly in the <color=#3366CC>north</color> and west, and the Dravidian in some parts of east India and most of the
<color=#3366CC>south</color>. <color=#3366CC>Classical Sanskrit</color>, a refined and standardised grammatical form would emerge in the mid-1st millennium BCE
and was codified in the Astādhyāyī ('Eight chapters') of <color=#3366CC>Pānini</color>. The two major Sanskrit epics, the <color=#3366CC>Mahābhārata</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Rāmāyana</color>, however, were composed in a range of oral storytelling registers called Epic Sanskrit which was used in
northern India between 400 BCE and 300 CE, and roughly contemporary with classical Sanskrit.
A second <color=#3366CC>urbanisation</color> had taken place in <color=#3366CC>South Asia</color> by, this time on the Ganges plain. In fortified cities, social
differentiation by <color=#3366CC>caste</color>, or varna, had emerged. By the mid-millennium two new ethical and social systems had arisen:
<color=#3366CC>Jainism</color> based on the teachings of <color=#3366CC>Mahavira</color> and Buddhism on those of <color=#3366CC>the Buddha</color>. Both religions stressed
non-violence and abjured animal sacrifices conducted in <color=#3366CC>Brahmanism</color>, and birth into a fixed hereditary varna. By living
ethically, lay people could rise socially and morally in these religions. Chronicling the life of the Buddha was central to
the beginnings of recorded history in India. The rise of the two religions was a backdrop to the emergence of the first
loose-knit geographically extensive power in South Asia, the <color=#3366CC>Maurya Empire</color>. During the rule of the founder's grandson,
<color=#3366CC>Ashoka</color> (ca. 268–232 BCE), the empire briefly controlled the major urban hubs and arteries of the subcontinent, except
in the deep south. The empire's period was notable for creativity in art, architecture, inscriptions, and produced texts,
but also for the declining rights of women in the mainstream <color=#3366CC>Indo-Aryan speaking</color> regions. Following his <color=#3366CC>conquest of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kalinga</color>, in which his forces caused immense loss of life, Ashoka adopted <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, subsequently adopting a policy of
dhamma and commissioning numerous <color=#3366CC>rock and pillar edicts</color> throughout the Maurya Empire to promote ethical
conduct, non-violence, and social welfare. As the edicts forbade both the killing of wild animals and the destruction of
forests, Ashoka is seen by some modern environmental historians as an early embodiment of that ethos.
By the 4th and 5th centuries, the <color=#3366CC>Gupta Empire</color> had created a complex system of administration and taxation in the
greater Ganges Plain; this system became a model for later Indian kingdoms. Under the Guptas, a renewed Hinduism
based on devotion, rather than the management of ritual, began to assert itself. The renewal was reflected in a
flowering of art, literature, and science. In South India, the Sangam literature of the <color=#3366CC>Tamil language</color> reveals that,
between and 200, the southern peninsula was ruled by the <color=#3366CC>Cheras</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Cholas</color>, along the western and eastern
plains, respectively, of the <color=#3366CC>Kaveri river</color> valley, and the <color=#3366CC>Pandyas</color> farther south along the Vaigai river valley. By the sixth
century, the <color=#3366CC>Pallavas</color> had grown into a regional power. Simultaneously, Buddhism and Jainism, which had favoured a
conservative transactionalism, were replaced by kingly devotion to the gods of particular places, which became a
characteristic of the Bhakti movement. The Pallavas, in particular, traded extensively with the Roman Empire and with
<color=#3366CC>West</color> and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>.
Medieval India
The Indian early medieval age, from 600 to 1200, was defined by regional kingdoms and cultural diversity. No ruler of
this period was able to create an empire and consistently control lands much beyond their core region. During this time,
pastoral peoples, whose land had been cleared to make way for the growing agricultural economy, were
accommodated within caste society, as were new non-traditional ruling classes. The caste system consequently began
to show regional differences.
In the 6th and 7th centuries, the first devotional hymns were composed in Tamil. They were imitated all over India and
led to both the resurgence of Hinduism and the development of all modern languages of the subcontinent. Indian
royalty, big and small, and the temples they patronised drew citizens in significant numbers to the capital cities, which
became economic hubs as well. Temple towns of various sizes began to appear everywhere as India underwent
another urbanisation. By the 8th and 9th centuries, the effects were felt in Southeast Asia, as South Indian culture and

political systems were exported to lands that became part of modern-day <color=#3366CC>Myanmar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thailand</color>, <color=#3366CC>Laos</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brunei</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cambodia</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Vietnam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>, <color=#3366CC>Malaysia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>. Indian merchants, scholars, and sometimes armies were involved in this
transmission; Southeast Asians took the initiative as well, with many sojourning in Indian seminaries and translating
Buddhist and Hindu texts into their languages.
After the 10th century, Muslim Central Asian nomadic clans, using swift-horse cavalry and raising vast armies united by
ethnicity, repeatedly overran South Asia's north-western plains, leading eventually to the establishment of the Islamic
<color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color> in 1206. The sultanate was to control much of North India and to make many forays into South India.
Although at first disruptive for the Indian elites, the sultanate largely left its vast non-Muslim subject population to its
own laws and customs.
By repeatedly repulsing <color=#3366CC>Mongol raiders</color> in the 13th century, the sultanate saved India from the devastation visited on
West and Central Asia, setting the scene for centuries of <color=#3366CC>migration</color> of fleeing soldiers, learned men, mystics, traders,
artists, and artisans from that region into the subcontinent, thereby creating a syncretic Indo-Islamic culture in the north.
The sultanate's raiding and weakening of the regional kingdoms of South India paved the way for the indigenous
<color=#3366CC>Vijayanagara Empire</color>. Embracing a strong <color=#3366CC>Shaivite</color> tradition and building upon the military technology of the sultanate,
the empire came to control a large portion of peninsular India, and was to influence South Indian society for long
afterwards.
Early modern India
In the early 16th century, northern India—then mainly under Muslim rulers,—fell again to the superior mobility and
firepower of a new generation of Central Asian warriors. The resulting <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> did not stamp out the local
societies it came to rule. Instead, it balanced and pacified them through new administrative practices and diverse and
inclusive ruling elites. This led to more systematic, centralised, and uniform rule. By departing from tribal bonds and
exclusive Islamic identity, particularly under Akbar, the Mughals united their vast empire through personal loyalty to a
near-divine emperor. It was expressed through a shared Persianised culture.
The Mughal state derived most revenue from agriculture. Its economic policies mandated tax payments in a
well-regulated silver currency, and integrated peasants and artisans into larger markets. The relative peace maintained
by the empire across much of the 17th century was a factor in India's economic expansion. Mughal ruling classes
fostered extensive patronage of the arts, including painting, literary forms, textiles, and architecture. Newly coherent
social groups in northern and western India, such as the <color=#3366CC>Marathas</color>, the Rajputs, and the <color=#3366CC>Sikhs</color>, gained governing
ambitions during Mughal rule. Through collaboration or adversity, the Mughals gave them recognition and military
experience. Expanding commerce gave rise to new Indian commercial and political elites along the coasts of southern
and eastern India. From the late 17th century, the Mughal empire gradually began to disintegrate, and these local elites
and communities frequently gained greater autonomy and self-governance.
By the early 18th century, the lines between commercial enterprise and political sovereignty had become increasingly
blurred. European chartered companies solidified their presence in India through fortified coastal outposts; most
notable was the <color=#3366CC>English East India Company</color>. Its control of the seas, greater resources, and more advanced military
training and technology led it to assert its military strength increasingly and caused it to become attractive to a portion
of the Indian elite; these factors were crucial in allowing the company to gain control over the <color=#3366CC>Bengal</color> region by 1765
and sideline the other European companies. Its further access to the riches of Bengal and the subsequent increased
strength and size of its army enabled it to annexe or subdue most of India by the 1820s. India no longer exported
manufactured goods as it had long, but instead supplied the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> with raw materials. Many historians
consider this to be the onset of India's colonial period. By this time, with its economic power severely curtailed by the
British Parliament and having effectively been made an arm of British administration, the East India Company began
more consciously to enter non-economic arenas, including education, social reform, and culture.
Modern India
The appointment in 1848 of Lord Dalhousie as Governor General of the East India Company set the stage for changes
essential to a modern state: the consolidation and demarcation of sovereignty, the surveillance of the population, and
the education of citizens. Technological changes—among them, railways, canals, and the telegraph—were introduced
not long after their introduction in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. Disaffection with the company also grew during this time, culminating in the
<color=#3366CC>Indian Rebellion of 1857</color>. Fed by diverse resentments and perceptions, including invasive British-style social reforms,
harsh land taxes, and summary treatment of some wealthy landowners and princes, the rebellion rocked many regions
of northern and central India and shook the foundations of Company rule. After the rebellion was suppressed in 1858,
the East India Company was disbanded, and the British government began to <color=#3366CC>directly administer India</color>. Proclaiming a
<color=#3366CC>unitary state</color> and a gradual but limited British-style parliamentary system, the new rulers also protected princes and
landed gentry as a feudal safeguard against future unrest. In the decades following, public life gradually emerged
across India, eventually leading to the founding of the <color=#3366CC>Indian National Congress</color> in 1885.
The rush of technology and the commercialisation of agriculture during the second half of the 19th century was marked
by economic setbacks, and many small farmers became dependent on the whims of faraway markets. There was an
increase in the number of large-scale famines, and, despite the risks of infrastructure development borne by Indian
taxpayers, little industrial employment was generated for Indians. However, commercial cropping, especially in the
newly canalled Punjab, led to increased food production for internal consumption. The railway network provided critical
famine relief, notably reduced the cost of moving goods, and helped nascent Indian-owned industry.
After <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, in which more than 1.3 million Indians served, a new period began. It was marked by British reforms
but also repressive legislation, by more strident Indian calls for self-rule, and by the beginnings of a <color=#3366CC>nonviolent</color>
movement of non-co-operation led by <color=#3366CC>Mahatma Gandhi</color>. During the 1930s, the British enacted slow legislative reform;
the Indian National Congress won victories in the resulting elections. The next decade was beset with crises: Indian
participation in World War II, the Congress's final push for non-co-operation, and an upsurge of Muslim nationalism. All
were capped by the advent of independence in 1947, but tempered by the <color=#3366CC>partition of India</color> into two states: India and
Pakistan.
India's constitution was adopted in 1950 and established a secular, democratic republic. Economic liberalisation has
created a large urban middle class and transformed India into a fast growing economy. However, India has been
hamstrung by persistent poverty, both rural and urban; <color=#3366CC>religious</color>- and caste-related violence; <color=#3366CC>Maoist-inspired Naxalite</color>
<color=#3366CC>insurgencies</color>; and separatism in Jammu and Kashmir and in Northeast India. India has unresolved territorial disputes
with China and with <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color>.
Geography
India accounts for the bulk of the Indian subcontinent, lying atop the Indian tectonic plate, and a part of the
<color=#3366CC>Indo-Australian Plate</color>. India's defining geologic processes began approximately 70 million years ago, when the Indian
Plate, then part of the southern supercontinent <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>, began a north-eastward <color=#3366CC>drift</color> caused by seafloor spreading
to its south-west, and later, south and south-east. Simultaneously, the vast <color=#3366CC>Tethyan</color> <color=#3366CC>oceanic crust</color>, to its northeast,
began to <color=#3366CC>subduct</color> under the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian Plate</color>. The Indian continental crust, however, was obstructed and was sheared
horizontally. Its lower crust and mantle slid under, but the upper layer piled up in sheets (or nappes) ahead of the
subduction zone. This created the <color=#3366CC>orogeny</color>, or process of mountain building, of the Himalayas. The middle and stiffer
layer continued to push into Tibet, causing crustal thickening of the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Plateau</color>. Immediately south of the emerging
Himalayas, plate movement created a vast crescent-shaped trough that rapidly filled with river-borne sediment and now
constitutes the <color=#3366CC>Indo-Gangetic Plain</color>. The original Indian plate makes its first appearance above the sediment in the
ancient Aravalli range, which extends from the Delhi Ridge in a southwesterly direction. To the west lies the <color=#3366CC>Thar</color>
<color=#3366CC>Desert</color>, the eastern spread of which is checked by the Aravallis.
The remaining Indian Plate survives as <color=#3366CC>peninsular India</color>, the oldest and geologically most stable part of India. It extends
as far north as the Satpura and Vindhya ranges in central India. These parallel chains run from the Arabian Sea coast
in Gujarat in the west to the coal-rich Chota Nagpur Plateau in Jharkhand in the east. To the south, the remaining
peninsular landmass, the <color=#3366CC>Deccan Plateau</color>, is flanked on the west and east by coastal ranges known as the <color=#3366CC>Western</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Eastern Ghats</color>; the plateau contains the country's oldest rock formations, some over one billion years old.
Constituted in such fashion, India lies to the north of the equator between 6° 44′ and 35° 30′ north latitude and 68° 7′
and 97° 25′ east longitude.
Major Himalayan-origin rivers that substantially flow through India include the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Brahmaputra</color>, both of
which drain into the <color=#3366CC>Bay of Bengal</color>. Important tributaries of the Ganges include the <color=#3366CC>Yamuna</color> and the Kosi. The Kosi's
extremely low gradient, caused by long-term silt deposition, leads to severe floods and course changes. Major
peninsular rivers, whose steeper gradients prevent their waters from flooding, include the <color=#3366CC>Godavari</color>, the Mahanadi, the
<color=#3366CC>Kaveri</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Krishna</color>, which also drain into the Bay of Bengal; and the <color=#3366CC>Narmada</color> and the Tapti, which drain into the
<color=#3366CC>Arabian Sea</color>.
India's coastline measures 7517 km in length; of this distance, 5423 km belong to peninsular India and 2094 km to the
Andaman, Nicobar, and Lakshadweep island chains. According to the Indian naval hydrographic charts, the mainland
coastline consists of the following: 43% sandy beaches; 11% rocky shores, including cliffs; and 46% <color=#3366CC>mudflats</color> or
marshy shores. Coastal features include the marshy Rann of Kutch of western India and the alluvial <color=#3366CC>Sundarbans</color> delta
of eastern India; the latter is shared with Bangladesh. India has two <color=#3366CC>archipelagos</color>: the <color=#3366CC>Lakshadweep</color> <color=#3366CC>coral atolls</color> off
India's south-western coast; and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, a volcanic chain in the <color=#3366CC>Andaman Sea</color>.
India has 28 states and 8 union territories.
Climate
The Indian climate is strongly influenced by the Himalayas and the Thar Desert, both of which drive the economically
and culturally pivotal summer and winter <color=#3366CC>monsoons</color>. The Himalayas prevent cold Central Asian <color=#3366CC>katabatic winds</color> from
blowing in, keeping the bulk of the Indian subcontinent warmer than most locations at similar latitudes. The Thar Desert
plays a crucial role in attracting the moisture-laden south-west summer monsoon winds that, between June and
October, provide the majority of India's rainfall.
Four major climatic groupings predominate in India: tropical wet, tropical dry, subtropical humid, and montane.
Temperatures in India have risen by 0.7 C-change between 1901 and 2018. <color=#3366CC>Climate change in India</color> is often thought to
be the cause. The retreat of Himalayan glaciers has adversely affected the <color=#3366CC>flow rate</color> of the major Himalayan rivers,
including the <color=#3366CC>Ganges</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Brahmaputra</color>. According to some current projections, the number and severity of
droughts in India will have markedly increased by the end of the present century.
Biodiversity
India is a megadiverse country, a term employed for 17 countries that host high <color=#3366CC>biological diversity</color> and contain many

species indigenous, or <color=#3366CC>endemic</color>, to them. India is the <color=#3366CC>habitat</color> for 8.6% of all <color=#3366CC>mammals</color>, 13.7% of <color=#3366CC>bird</color> species, 7.9% of

<color=#3366CC>reptile</color> species, 6% of <color=#3366CC>amphibian</color> species, 12.2% of <color=#3366CC>fish</color> species, and 6.0% of all <color=#3366CC>flowering plant</color> species. Fully a third of
Indian plant species are endemic. India also overlaps four of the world's 34 biodiversity hotspots, or regions that display
significant habitat loss in the presence of high endemism.

India's most dense forests, such as the <color=#3366CC>tropical moist forest</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Andaman Islands</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Western Ghats</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Northeast</color>
<color=#3366CC>India</color>, occupy approximately 3% of its land area. Moderately dense forest, whose canopy density is between 40% and
70%, occupies 9.39% of India's land area. It predominates in the <color=#3366CC>temperate coniferous forest</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color>, the
moist deciduous sal forest of eastern India, and the dry deciduous <color=#3366CC>teak</color> forest of central and southern India. India has
two natural zones of <color=#3366CC>thorn forest</color>, one in the <color=#3366CC>Deccan Plateau</color>, immediately east of the Western Ghats, and the other in
the western part of the Indo-Gangetic plain, now turned into rich agricultural land by irrigation, its features no longer
visible. Among the Indian subcontinent's notable indigenous trees are the astringent <color=#3366CC>Azadirachta indica</color>, or neem, which
is widely used in rural Indian <color=#3366CC>herbal medicine</color>, and the luxuriant Ficus religiosa, or peepul, which is displayed on the
ancient seals of <color=#3366CC>Mohenjo-daro</color>, and under which <color=#3366CC>the Buddha</color> is recorded in the <color=#3366CC>Pali canon</color> to have sought
enlightenment.
Many Indian species have descended from those of <color=#3366CC>Gondwana</color>, the southern <color=#3366CC>supercontinent</color> from which India
separated more than 100 million years ago. India's subsequent collision with Eurasia set off a mass exchange of
species. However, <color=#3366CC>volcanism</color> and <color=#3366CC>climatic changes</color> later caused the extinction of many endemic Indian forms. Still later,
mammals entered India from Asia through two zoogeographic passes flanking the Himalayas. This lowered endemism
among India's mammals, which stands at 12.6%, contrasting with 45.8% among reptiles and 55.8% among
amphibians. Among endemics are the vulnerable hooded leaf monkey and the threatened Beddome's toad of the
Western Ghats.
India contains 172 <color=#3366CC>IUCN</color>-designated threatened animal species, or 2.9% of endangered forms. These include the
endangered <color=#3366CC>Bengal tiger</color> and the Ganges river dolphin. Critically endangered species include the <color=#3366CC>gharial</color>, a <color=#3366CC>crocodilian</color>;
the great Indian bustard; and the Indian white-rumped vulture, which has become nearly extinct by having ingested the
carrion of diclofenac-treated cattle. Before they were extensively used for agriculture and cleared for human settlement,
the thorn forests of Punjab were mingled at intervals with open grasslands that were grazed by large herds of
blackbuck preyed on by the Asiatic cheetah; the blackbuck, no longer extant in Punjab, is now severely endangered in
India, and the cheetah is extinct. The pervasive and ecologically devastating human encroachment of recent decades
has critically endangered Indian wildlife. In response, the system of national parks and protected areas, first established
in 1935, was expanded substantially. In 1972, India enacted the Wildlife Protection Act and Project Tiger to safeguard
crucial wilderness; the Forest Conservation Act was enacted in 1980 and amendments added in 1988. India hosts
more than five hundred wildlife sanctuaries and eighteen biosphere reserves, four of which are part of the World
Network of Biosphere Reserves; its eighty-nine wetlands are registered under the Ramsar Convention.
Government and politics
Politics
India is a parliamentary republic with a multi-party system. There are six recognised national parties in the country,
including the <color=#3366CC>Indian National Congress</color> (generally, "the Congress") and the <color=#3366CC>Bharatiya Janata Party</color> (BJP); there are
over 50 regional parties. The Congress is considered the <color=#3366CC>ideological centre</color> in Indian political culture; the BJP is
<color=#3366CC>right-wing</color> to <color=#3366CC>far-right</color>. Following independence on August 15, 1947, Jawaharlal Nehru served as prime minister of the
Dominion of India, remaining caretaker until 1951, shortly after India became a republic in 1950. Led by Nehru, the
Congress won the 1951, 1957, and 1962 general elections comfortably. After Nehru died in May 1964, <color=#3366CC>Lal Bahadur</color>
<color=#3366CC>Shastri</color> became prime minister. Shastri passed away in January 1966, shortly after signing the Tashkent Peace
Declaration following the India–Pakistan war of 1965.
The Congress chose <color=#3366CC>Indira Gandhi</color> as prime minister, leading the party to election victories in 1967 and 1971. In 1975,
she declared a <color=#3366CC>state of emergency</color>, suspending civil liberties, which led to Congress being voted out in 1977. The
opposing Janata Party government lasted two years under <color=#3366CC>Morarji Desai</color> and <color=#3366CC>Charan Singh</color>, before Congress returned

to power in 1980. Following a <color=#3366CC>military operation</color> at the <color=#3366CC>Golden Temple</color> in <color=#3366CC>Amritsar</color>, Indira Gandhi was <color=#3366CC>assassinated</color> by
her Sikh bodyguard on October 31, 1984. Indira Gandhi's son, <color=#3366CC>Rajiv Gandhi</color>, succeeded her and won the late 1984
elections. In 1989, a National Front coalition won the general elections, forming a two-year government led by V. P.
Singh and Chandra Shekhar. During the general election, Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by a Sri Lankan Tamil
separatist. Congress emerged from the elections as the largest party, and <color=#3366CC>P. V. Narasimha Rao</color> formed a minority
government that completed a full five-year term.
In 1996, after winning the general election, the BJP briefly formed a government before United Front governments took
over under H. D. Deve Gowda and I. K. Gujral. After the 1998 Indian general election, the BJP’s <color=#3366CC>Atal Bihari Vajpayee</color>
became prime minister, but his initial government was short-lived. Following the 1999 elections, Vajpayee led a
National Democratic Alliance (NDA) coalition, becoming the first non-Congress prime minister to complete a five-year
term. The NDA was defeated in 2004 by the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance (UPA). Proposed by <color=#3366CC>Sonia</color>
<color=#3366CC>Gandhi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Manmohan Singh</color> served as prime minister with external support, returning with increased, independent
numbers in 2009. Singh was the first prime minister re-elected since Nehru in 1962.
In 2014, the BJP led by <color=#3366CC>Narendra Modi</color> won an absolute majority, in the Indian parliament, and expanded it in 2019.
The party joined an NDA coalition after losing its single-party majority in the 2024 general election. Modi remains the
longest-serving non-Congress prime minister.
Government
The Constitution of India was drafted by the Constituent Assembly of India with uncommon speed and absence of
irregularities between 1946 and 1949. The Government of India Act 1935 was used as a model and framework. Long
passages from the Act were included. The constitution describes a federal state with a parliamentary system of
democracy. The federal structure was conspicuous for the strength of the central government, which exclusively
exercised control of defence, foreign affairs, railways, ports, and currency. The President, the constitutional head of
state, has reserve powers for taking over the administration of a state. The central legislature has two houses: the Lok
Sabha, whose delegates are directly elected by the people in general elections every five years, and the Rajya Sabha,
whose members are nominated by the elected representatives in the states. There are also features not to be found in
the Act of 1935. The definition of fundamental rights is based on the <color=#3366CC>Constitution of the United States</color>, and the
constitutional directives, or goals of endeavour, are based on the Constitution of Ireland. An Indian institution
recommended by the constitution is the panchayat or village committees. Untouchability is illegal (Article 17) and caste
distinctions are derecognised (Articles 15(2) and 16(2)). The promulgation of the Indian constitution transformed India
into a republic within the Commonwealth.
The prime minister of India is the <color=#3366CC>head of government</color> and exercises most <color=#3366CC>executive power</color>. Appointed by the president,
the prime minister is supported by the <color=#3366CC>party</color> or political alliance with a majority of seats in the lower house of parliament.
The executive of the Indian government consists of the president, the vice-president, and the Union Council of
Ministers—with the <color=#3366CC>cabinet</color> being its executive committee—headed by the prime minister. Any minister holding a
portfolio must be a member of one of the houses of parliament. In the Indian parliamentary system, the executive is
subordinate to the legislature; the prime minister and their council are directly responsible to the lower house of the
parliament. Civil servants act as permanent executives and all decisions of the executive are implemented by them.
India has a three-tier unitary <color=#3366CC>independent judiciary</color> comprising the <color=#3366CC>supreme court</color>, headed by the Chief Justice of India,
25 high courts, and a large number of trial courts. The supreme court has original jurisdiction over cases involving
fundamental rights and over disputes between states and the centre and has appellate jurisdiction over the high courts.
It has the power to both strike down union or state laws which contravene the constitution and invalidate any
government action it deems unconstitutional.
Administrative divisions
India is a federal union comprising 28 states and 8 union territories. All states, as well as the union territories of <color=#3366CC>Jammu</color>
<color=#3366CC>and Kashmir</color>, Puducherry and the <color=#3366CC>National Capital Territory of Delhi</color>, have elected legislatures and governments
following the Westminster system. The remaining five union territories are directly ruled by the central government
through appointed administrators. In 1956, under the States Reorganisation Act, states were reorganised on a linguistic
basis. There are over a quarter of a million local government bodies at city, town, district, block and village levels.

Foreign relations
India remained a member of the <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth of Nations</color> after becoming a republic in 1950. It strongly supported
decolonisation in Africa and Asia in the 1950s, and played a leading role in the Non-Aligned Movement. After cordial
relations with China during the greater part of the 1950s, India and China went to <color=#3366CC>war in 1962</color>; India was widely thought
to have been decisively defeated. By 1967, however, India was able to fend off Chinese excursions into Sikkim.
India has had uneasy relations with its western neighbour, Pakistan. The two went to war in 1947, 1965, <color=#3366CC>1971</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>1999</color>. Three wars were fought over the <color=#3366CC>disputed territory of Kashmir</color>. After the 1965 war, India began to pursue close
military and economic ties with the Soviet Union. By the late 1960s, the Soviet Union was India's largest arms supplier.
China's nuclear test of 1964 and threats to intervene in support of Pakistan in the 1965 war caused India to produce
nuclear weapons. India conducted its first nuclear weapons test in 1974 and carried out additional underground testing
in 1998. India has signed neither the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty nor the Nuclear Non-Proliferation
Treaty, considering both to be flawed and discriminatory. India maintains a "no first use" nuclear policy and possesses
a nuclear triad as a part of its "Minimum Credible Deterrence" doctrine.
Since the end of the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>, India has increased its economic, strategic, and military cooperation with the United
States and the European Union. In 2008, a civilian nuclear agreement was signed between India and the United States.
Although India possessed nuclear weapons at the time and was not a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, it
received waivers from the <color=#3366CC>International Atomic Energy Agency</color> and the Nuclear Suppliers Group, ending earlier
restrictions on India's nuclear technology and commerce; India subsequently signed co-operation agreements involving
civilian nuclear energy with Russia, France, the United Kingdom, and Canada.
Economy
Economic history
The economic history of colonial India and early postcolonial India began with colonial extraction and ended with state
planning. During <color=#3366CC>British rule</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Indian subcontinent</color> underwent <color=#3366CC>deindustrialisation</color>. After India's independence in 1947,
it adopted a socialist-oriented <color=#3366CC>economic model</color> that relied on government-owned heavy industries and five-year plans
which took their cues from those of the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> of the 1930s. Although the Green Revolution of the 1960s
eventually helped India to attain some <color=#3366CC>self-sufficiency</color> in food, India's economic growth in real terms remained low. A
<color=#3366CC>balance of payments</color> crisis in 1991 forced the government's hand, and led it to embracing economic deregulation. The
reduction in the government's control over the economy opened the domestic market to foreign direct investment and
sped up the growth of <color=#3366CC>private enterprise</color>.
Modern economy
Today, India is a large emerging market with strong <color=#3366CC>local buying</color>. Its expanding <color=#3366CC>economic output</color> ranks among the
largest in the world both by <color=#3366CC>market exchange rates</color> and <color=#3366CC>purchasing power parity</color>. Although <color=#3366CC>agricultural production</color>
remains the main source of employment for nearly half the population, the overall economy is led predominantly by the
service sector. India relies on financial technology, <color=#3366CC>information systems</color>, and professional services both for its export
earnings and <color=#3366CC>urban development</color>. Recent government initiatives have emphasized <color=#3366CC>physical infrastructure</color> and
manufacturing programmes designed to increase indigenous industrial capacity.
Even though India's economy is strong and expanding rapidly, it wrestles with problems built into the very foundation of
its system. The per capita income remains low relative to other large emerging economies, and shows large
imbalances in the distribution of wealth. The official <color=#3366CC>labour market</color> struggles to generate enough stable jobs to account
for the expanding, youthful, workforce; this leaves a large proportion of the population to rely on <color=#3366CC>informal employment</color>.
Significant gaps exist in regional growth within India: less developed states lag considerably behind advanced cities in
human capital development and how swiftly their governments can clamp down on those who flout rules and
regulations.
Industries
India is a worldwide centre for <color=#3366CC>information technology</color> and business services, which add 7.5% to GDP and over 35% to
<color=#3366CC>services sold abroad</color>. This sector is sustained by a large English-speaking skilled labour force, with revenues
surpassing $300 billion in Fiscal Year 2026. Although the industry once relied on basic call centres and simple software
fixes, it has shifted toward <color=#3366CC>cloud computing</color>, <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color>, and international tech hubs. <color=#3366CC>Bangalore</color> has grown
from a cheap offshore site into a top centre for corporate research, making it the largest technology hub outside <color=#3366CC>Silicon</color>
<color=#3366CC>Valley</color>.
India's automotive sector comprises 7.1% of its economy. It produces 28 million vehicles every year of which the vast
majority are two-wheelers (77%) followed by <color=#3366CC>passenger cars</color> (18%). Of every 1000 Indians, 34 own cars and 185 own
two-wheelers. The industry provides 19 million jobs and sells 5.3 million vehicles abroad annually. In 2023, India
became the third-largest automobile market in the world, with buyers, many of whom are in their 30s, increasingly
preferring SUVs.
The Indian pharmaceutical sector relies on a vast network of production facilities focused on low-cost manufacturing.
Thousands of individual factories and domestic firms comprise this sector and together make India the main worldwide
source of generic medications and vaccines by volume. However, the sector faces supply line vulnerabilities, especially
a reliance on China for over 70% of its raw active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). It also faces international
quality-control audits in its factories.
India's capacity to generate electrical power is 300 gigawatts, of which 42 gigawatts is renewable. The country's usage
of coal is a major cause of <color=#3366CC>India's greenhouse gas emissions</color>, but its renewable energy capacity is growing. India emits
about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions. This equates to about 2.5 tonnes of <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color> per person per year,
which is half the world average. Increasing <color=#3366CC>access to electricity</color> and clean cooking with <color=#3366CC>liquefied petroleum gas</color> have
been priorities for energy in India.
Demographics
With an estimated 1,428,627,663 residents in 2023, India is the world's most populous country. 1,210,193,422
residents were reported in the 2011 provisional census report. The median age was 28.7 in 2020. Medical advances
made in the last 50 years as well as increased agricultural productivity brought about by the "Green Revolution" have
caused India's population to grow rapidly, though India's decennial rates of growth are decreasing: its population grew
by 17.64% from 2001 to 2011, compared to 21.54% growth in the previous decade (1991–2001). The first post-colonial
census, conducted in 1951, counted 361 million people. The <color=#3366CC>life expectancy</color> at birth has increased from 49.7 years in
1970–1975 to 72.0 years in 2023. The under-five <color=#3366CC>mortality</color> rate for the country was 113 per 1,000 live births in 1994,
and had declined to 41.1 per 1,000 live births by 2018.
The human sex ratio, according to the 2011 census, is 940 females per 1,000 males. Female infanticide in India, and
lately female foeticide, have created lop-sided gender ratios; the number of missing women in the country quadrupled
from 15 million to 63 million during the period 1964–2014, faster than the population growth during the same period.
According to an Indian government study, an additional 21 million girls are unwanted and do not receive adequate care.
Despite a government ban on sex-selective foeticide, the practice has far from stopped.
Migration from rural to urban areas has been an important dynamic in India's recent history. The number of people
living in urban areas grew by 31.2% between 1991 and 2001. In 2001, over 70% lived in rural areas. The level of
urbanisation increased further from 27.81% in the 2001 census to 31.16% in the 2011 census. The slowing down of the
overall population growth rate was due to the sharp decline in the growth rate in rural areas since 1991. In the 2011

census, there were 53 million-plus urban agglomerations in India, among them <color=#3366CC>Mumbai</color>, <color=#3366CC>Delhi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kolkata</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chennai</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Bangalore</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hyderabad</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ahmedabad</color>, in decreasing order by population.
Languages

government, gives the following breakdown:
There are also small numbers of speakers of <color=#3366CC>Tai–Kadai</color>, Andamanese, and minor language families and <color=#3366CC>isolates</color>.
The official language of India's federal government was chosen by the Constituent Assembly of India in September
1949 after three years of debate between two opposing camps. <color=#3366CC>Hindi language</color> protagonists wanted Hindi in the
<color=#3366CC>Devanagari script</color> to be the sole "national language" of India whereas delegates from South India preferred English to
have a place in the Constitution. The compromise reached declared (i) Hindi to be the "official language" of India's
federal government; (ii) English to be an associate official language for 15 years during which Hindi's formal lexicon
would be developed; and (iii) the international form of <color=#3366CC>Hindu–Arabic numerals</color> to be the official numerals. The
compromise resolution became articles 343–351 of India's constitution, which came into effect on 26 January 1950. In
1965, after bitter opposition from <color=#3366CC>South India</color> to Hindi becoming the sole official language, a compromise was reached
to where English would continue to be an "associate official language" indefinitely.
The Eighth Schedule of India's Constitution also recognises 22 languages, including Hindi but not English, which the
government is obligated to develop. These are sometimes called "scheduled languages". This list includes major
regional languages, but also others—such as <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color>, which no longer has <color=#3366CC>first language</color> speakers in India, and <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color>,
which is not region-specific—because of their value to India's cultural heritage. In 1950, there were 14 scheduled

languages: <color=#3366CC>Assamese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bengali</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gujarati</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hindi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kannada</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kashmiri</color>, <color=#3366CC>Malayalam</color>, <color=#3366CC>Marathi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Oriya</color>, <color=#3366CC>Punjabi</color>, Sanskrit,

<color=#3366CC>Tamil</color>, <color=#3366CC>Telugu</color> and Urdu. In the following decades constitutional amendments added others: <color=#3366CC>Sindhi</color> (1967), <color=#3366CC>Nepali</color>,
Manipuri, and Konkani (1992), <color=#3366CC>Maithili</color>, Dogri, Santali and Bodo (2004).
Religion
India has had a long history of religious pluralism that shapes its modern society. Hinduism is the majority faith followed
by nearly 80% of the population; Islam is the largest minority at over 14%. Hinduism has many schools of thought, such
as those rooted in <color=#3366CC>Vedanta</color>; sacred texts such as the <color=#3366CC>Vedas</color>; and practices such as bhakti involving a personal
relationship with the deity. Islam in India has freewheeling <color=#3366CC>Sufi</color> traditions, but also more disciplined prayers at <color=#3366CC>mosques</color>.
India also has populations of <color=#3366CC>Christians</color> and Sikhs in the tens of millions; Buddhists and <color=#3366CC>Jains</color> in lower millions; as well
as dwindling populations of <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrians</color> and <color=#3366CC>Jews</color>. The Saint Thomas Christians in South India trace their history to
the arrival ashore in India of <color=#3366CC>St Thomas the Apostle</color> in the 1st century CE; they have their distinctive <color=#3366CC>liturgical traditions</color>.
India's western coast has Zoroastrians, or Parsis, who worship at fire temples, and aging Jewish communities in Kerala
and Maharashtra, whose historic <color=#3366CC>synagogues</color> are tourist attractions. India is a secular state and guarantees the
<color=#3366CC>fundamental right</color> to <color=#3366CC>freedom of religion</color> ("Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship").
A large majority of Indian Muslims, Christians, and Sikhs participate in customs, or hold dear beliefs, that were once
only a part of Hinduism (e.g. <color=#3366CC>karma</color>). Sikh <color=#3366CC>gurdwaras</color> and Sufi dargahs often attract both visitors and worshippers from
other religions. India has monastic traditions such as that of Jain ascetics some of whom practice an extreme form of
<color=#3366CC>nonviolence</color> (<color=#3366CC>ahimsa</color>) and Buddhist <color=#3366CC>communities</color> who have preserved ancient styles of meditations. The religious
kaleidoscope coexists with religious <color=#3366CC>endogamy</color>—people rarely marry outside their faith—and religious segregation in
housing—many religious groups live together either by choice or by the lack of a better option; thus India's religious
picture has both intermixing and clear divisions.
Birth rates, <color=#3366CC>population growth</color>, and access to education commonly vary across religions. These influence how
communities mobilise politically to preserve their <color=#3366CC>places of worship</color>, to manage charitable trusts, and to protect their
family laws. Differences in states' laws, especially those prohibiting <color=#3366CC>religious conversion</color>—usually from Hinduism to
other faiths—colour the daily lives of minority communities. Providing constitutional protections for <color=#3366CC>minorities</color> in the face
of majoritarian pressure remains a fraught challenge.
Education
In 1911, there were three primary schools for every ten villages in British India. Early literacy was low: It was 5% in
1891 (9% for men and 1% for women) and 7% in 1921 (12% for men and 2% for women). Historically, local diversity
limited literacy growth in India because caste and religious fragmentation reduced private spending. Literacy rates rose
to 18% in 1951 (27% for men and 9% for women) and 41% in 1981 (53% for men and 29% for women). By 2011,
literacy reached 74.04% (82.14% for men and 65.46% for women). They ranged from Kerala's 93.91% to Bihar's
63.82%. Meanwhile, rural gains reached twice the level of urban, narrowing the rural-urban gap from 21.2 percentage
points in 2001 to 16.1 in 2011.
The central, state, and local governments manage education in India. Every child between the ages of 6 and 14 has a
right to education, which is free and compulsory. Traditionally, children had spent eight years in primary school before
moving on to high school. In 2020, the National Education Policy changed this division to one based on developmental
stages: a foundational stage: five years of pre-school and standards 1–2, for ages 3–8; a preparatory stage: standards
3–5; a middle stage: standards 6–8; and a secondary stage: standards 9–12. Critics argue that the new plan, although
progressive, suffers from public underfunding and inadequate school infrastructure.
The first universities in India were founded in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras in the waning years of East India
Company rule. India now has one of the world's largest systems of post-secondary education. Recent college reforms
envisage offering more flexible degrees, creating online learning tools, and inviting foreign universities to set up
campuses in India. However, large gaps remain between rural and urban areas. School quality, campus building
conditions, and computer access vary substantially based on a student's gender and family's wealth. Poor job
prospects for graduates and uneven rule enforcement across different states have faced criticism from researchers and
the public alike.
Health
Since its 1947 independence, India has significantly reduced historically <color=#3366CC>endemic</color> diseases, though some remain
intractable. The country was certified smallpox-free in April 1977 following two years of surveillance after its last <color=#3366CC>Variola</color>
<color=#3366CC>major</color> case. It was officially certified polio-free by the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organisation</color> on March 27, 2014, after successfully
completing three consecutive years without recorded cases of wild poliovirus. In contrast, cholera remains <color=#3366CC>endemic</color> to
<color=#3366CC>Ganges-Meghna Delta</color> <color=#3366CC>estuaries</color>, resulting in seasonal outbreaks caused by monsoons and <color=#3366CC>water supply network</color>
shortcomings. <color=#3366CC>Tuberculosis</color> is a major concern; India bears a quarter of the global tuberculosis disease burden.
Historical <color=#3366CC>malaria</color> cases have dropped from millions to hundreds of thousands annually, but India experiences localised
seasonal increases caused by drug-resistant variants of the Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax <color=#3366CC>vectors</color>.
Patients in India often face a stark choice: use basic, free, publicly funded health care or pay high out-of-pocket fees for
better-equipped care from private doctors and hospitals. This divide is particularly severe outside cities, as public clinics
in rural areas rarely have enough doctors or nurses to meet local demands. When serious medical emergencies occur,
poorer families are often forced to sell land or take out high-interest loans to pay for private care. This resulting medical
debt pushes approximately 55 million people into poverty every year.
Long-term exposure to outdoor and indoor <color=#3366CC>air pollution</color> adds a major environmental risk to <color=#3366CC>public health</color> in India.

<color=#3366CC>Particulate matter</color> emissions from <color=#3366CC>vehicles</color> and <color=#3366CC>factories</color> are linked to a rise in <color=#3366CC>chronic</color> <color=#3366CC>respiratory diseases</color>, <color=#3366CC>strokes</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>cardiovascular disease</color>, together adding an estimated 1.7 million <color=#3366CC>premature deaths</color> annually. India's early
COVID-19 lockdown bought time to rapidly increase local testing and protective gear production; however, later waves
of the virus overwhelmed the healthcare system, leading to severe shortages of oxygen and intensive care beds.
Post-<color=#3366CC>pandemic</color> <color=#3366CC>epidemiological studies</color> estimate that cumulative excess deaths in India reached between 3.2 and 4.7
million.
Culture
Society
Although sometimes applied to other cultures and religions, caste is a uniquely Indian, and Hindu, social institution. All
Hindus fall broadly into four castes, or varnas: <color=#3366CC>Brahmin</color>, or priests, at the top; below them <color=#3366CC>Kshatriya</color>, or warriors; further
below, <color=#3366CC>Vaishya</color>, or merchants and farmers; and at the bottom, <color=#3366CC>Shudra</color>, or the service class. Outside the caste system,
and therefore of traditional Hinduism, lie people formerly called "outcastes" or "untouchables," and now scheduled
caste (a term used in India's constitution) or <color=#3366CC>Dalit</color>, a later self-description of pride, meaning "broken" or "downtrodden".
Each caste is further divided into sub-castes, or jatis, many of which are tied to occupations. The custom of <color=#3366CC>endogamy</color>,
or marrying within one's subcaste, however, makes caste a hereditary label, not of one occupational choice, and has
caused the caste system, therefore, to become entrenched. The Constituent Assembly of India abolished untouchability
in 1947, the <color=#3366CC>Republic of India</color> did more formally in 1950, and India has since enacted other anti-discriminatory laws and
social welfare initiatives related to caste. Still, caste-based inequality, discrimination, segregation, and violence persist.
Multi-generational <color=#3366CC>patrilineal</color> <color=#3366CC>joint families</color> have been the norm in India, though <color=#3366CC>nuclear families</color> are becoming common
in urban areas. A very large majority of Indians have their marriages arranged by their parents or family elders.
Marriage is thought to be for life; and the divorce rate is extremely low; less than one in a thousand marriages end in
divorce. Many women marry before reaching 18, which is their legal marriageable age; <color=#3366CC>child marriages</color> are not
uncommon, especially in rural areas. In large parts of Hindu northern India, moreover, a form of territorial <color=#3366CC>exogamy</color> is
observed in which a bride marries out of her natal village and her parents do not visit her in her married home; the
annual rite raksha bandhan, during which married women return to their <color=#3366CC>natal</color> homes, has served both to affirm bonds
with their natal families and offer a recourse in times of marital stress.
Muslims, India's largest religious minority, have contributed greatly to a shared, blended culture that deeply shaped
India’s classical music, literature, and celebrated architecture. Modern Indian Muslim society is highly diverse, divided
by local languages, distinct cultural backgrounds, and internal social classes. However, Indian Muslims have much
lower college enrollment, less access to banking services, and far fewer formal jobs than average. Additionally, due to
safety worries and unfair housing practices, many urban Muslims have been forced to move into separated
neighbourhoods that often lack basic public services. Muslim women face overlapping challenges caused by family
expecations, which sometimes restrict them from working outside their neighbourhood, and unfair treatment by local
public officials. Muslim families regularly see higher rates of child survival compared to other religious and social
groups.
Visual art
India has a very ancient tradition of art, which has exchanged many influences with the rest of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color>, especially in the

first millennium. During this period <color=#3366CC>Buddhist art</color> spread with Indian religions to <color=#3366CC>Central</color>, <color=#3366CC>East</color> and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, the
last also greatly influenced by Hindu art. Thousands of <color=#3366CC>seals from the Indus Valley civilisation</color> of the third millennium
BCE have been found, usually carved with animals, but also some with human figures. The Pashupati seal, excavated
in <color=#3366CC>Mohenjo-daro</color>, Pakistan, in 1928–29, is the best known. Virtually no art survives from a long period following the
Indus Valley Civilisation. Almost all surviving ancient Indian art thereafter is in various forms of religious sculpture in
durable materials, or coins. There was probably originally far more in wood, which is lost. In north India Mauryan art is
the first imperial movement.
Over the following centuries a distinctly Indian style of sculpting the human figure developed, with less interest in
articulating precise anatomy than ancient Greek sculpture but showing smoothly flowing forms expressing prana
("breath" or life-force). This is often complicated by the need to give figures multiple arms or heads, or represent
different genders on the left and right of figures, as with the Ardhanarishvara form of Shiva and <color=#3366CC>Parvati</color>.
Most of the earliest large sculpture is Buddhist, either excavated from Buddhist stupas such as <color=#3366CC>Sanchi</color>, Sarnath and
Amaravati, or is rock cut <color=#3366CC>reliefs</color> at sites such as <color=#3366CC>Ajanta</color>, Karla and <color=#3366CC>Ellora</color>. Hindu and Jain sites appear rather later. In
spite of this complex mixture of religious traditions, generally, the prevailing artistic style at any time and place has
been shared by the major religious groups, and sculptors probably usually served all communities. Gupta art, at its
peak c. 300 – c. 500, is often regarded as a classical period whose influence lingered for many centuries after; it saw a
new dominance of Hindu sculpture, as at the <color=#3366CC>Elephanta Caves</color>. Across the north, this became rather stiff and formulaic
after c. 800, though rich with finely carved detail in the surrounds of statues. But in the South, under the <color=#3366CC>Pallava</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Chola dynasties</color>, sculpture in both stone and bronze had a sustained period of great achievement; the large bronzes
with Shiva as Nataraja have become an iconic symbol of India.
Ancient paintings have only survived at a few sites, of which the crowded scenes of court life in the <color=#3366CC>Ajanta Caves</color> are
some of the most important. Painted manuscripts of religious texts survive from Eastern India from 10th century
onwards, most of the earliest being Buddhist and later Jain. These significantly influenced later artistic styles. The
Persian-derived Deccan painting, starting just before the Mughal miniature, between them give the first large body of
secular painting, with an emphasis on portraits, and the recording of princely pleasures and wars. The style spread to
Hindu courts, especially among the Rajputs, and developed a variety of styles, with the smaller courts often the most
innovative, with figures such as Nihâl Chand and Nainsukh. As a market developed among European residents, it was
supplied by Company painting by Indian artists with considerable Western influence. In the 19th century, cheap
Kalighat paintings of gods and everyday life, done on paper, were urban <color=#3366CC>folk art</color> from <color=#3366CC>Calcutta</color>, which later saw the
Bengal School of Art, reflecting the art colleges founded by the British, the first movement in modern Indian painting.
Mathematics
Significant mathematics began in India in the first millennium BCE. The Śulba Sūtras (literally, "Aphorisms of the
Chords" in Vedic Sanskrit) (c. 700–400 BCE) contain the earliest extant verbal expression of the <color=#3366CC>Pythagorean theorem</color>
(although very likely it had been known to the Old Babylonians.) All mathematical works were orally transmitted until
approximately 500 BCE; thereafter, they were transmitted both orally and in manuscript form. The oldest extant
mathematical document produced on the Indian subcontinent is the birch bark Bakhshali manuscript from the 7th
century CE.
In the classical period of Indian mathematics (400 CE to 1200 CE), important contributions were made by <color=#3366CC>Aryabhata</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Brahmagupta</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bhaskara II</color>, Varāhamihira, and <color=#3366CC>Madhava</color>. The <color=#3366CC>decimal number system</color> in use today was first recorded in
Indian mathematics. Indian mathematicians made early contributions to the study of the concept of zero as a number,

<color=#3366CC>negative numbers</color>, <color=#3366CC>arithmetic</color>, and <color=#3366CC>algebra</color>. <color=#3366CC>Trigonometry</color> was further advanced in India, and the modern definitions of
<color=#3366CC>sine</color> and <color=#3366CC>cosine</color> were developed there. These mathematical concepts were transmitted to the Middle East, China, and
Europe. A later landmark in Indian mathematics was the development of the <color=#3366CC>series</color> expansions for <color=#3366CC>trigonometric</color>
<color=#3366CC>functions</color> (sine, cosine, and <color=#3366CC>arc tangent</color>) by mathematicians of the Kerala school in the 15th century CE. Their work,
completed two centuries before the invention of <color=#3366CC>calculus</color> in Europe, provided the first example of a <color=#3366CC>power series</color>. In the
modern era <color=#3366CC>Srinivasa Ramanujan</color> made fundamental contributions to <color=#3366CC>number theory</color>.
Music
India contains a wide array of musical practices, including many different folk musics from different regions. <color=#3366CC>Indian</color>
<color=#3366CC>classical music</color> has Vedic origins, and split in the 13th century into the two main traditions of <color=#3366CC>Hindustani</color> and <color=#3366CC>Carnatic</color>
music. Hindustani is associated with North India and is more <color=#3366CC>improvisational</color>, featuring instruments such as the <color=#3366CC>sitar</color>
and <color=#3366CC>tabla</color>, and Carnatic is South Indian and more focused on written <color=#3366CC>compositions</color> such as the kriti, while both styles
contain common elements such as the <color=#3366CC>raga</color> melodic framework and <color=#3366CC>tala</color> rhythmic meter. Indian music has influenced
western genres, including <color=#3366CC>rock</color> and <color=#3366CC>jazz</color> musicians during the <color=#3366CC>1960s counterculture</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Indian film music</color> is music written for <color=#3366CC>Indian cinema</color>, generally composed by music directors and sung by playback
singers. Modern Indian pop takes influences from classical, folk, and western <color=#3366CC>pop music</color>.
Dance
Dance in India has drawn heavily from <color=#3366CC>Indian classical dance</color> traditions. Many of these in turn arose in temples or other
religious contexts. Their sponsorship and promotion, however, has continued in secular, modern India. India also has
local and modern dance traditions. Whether a dance is classical is determined by the Sangeet Natak Academi, the
Indian government's organisation for performing arts. Although more dances could perhaps meet the criteria for
classical, the Akademi has chosen eight.
The best-known classical dance is Bharatanatyam, which began in the temple dances of <color=#3366CC>Tamil</color> devadasis. Identified
with "prostitutes and courtesans", their dancing was formally banned in 1947. Concurrently, the dance was rehabilitated
as a "pure" art form, with Rukmini Devi Arundale as a prominent figure. A devdasi who went on to attain national and
international prominence was Thanjavur Balasaraswati. Some sources consider the dance-dramas Chhau of
<color=#3366CC>Jharkhand</color>, <color=#3366CC>West Bengal</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Odisha</color> and Yakshagana of <color=#3366CC>Karnataka</color> to also belong to the classical tradition.
Local dance traditions vary widely across India. In addition to the dance-dramas Chhau and Yakshagana, they include
dance-dramas Raslila of western <color=#3366CC>Uttar Pradesh</color> and Terukkuttu of Tamil Nadu; calendrical and festival dances such as
the <color=#3366CC>Bhangra</color> of Punjab, especially at Vaisakhi, the onset of spring, and Garba of <color=#3366CC>Gujarat</color> during Navratri; and tribal or
<color=#3366CC>Adivasi</color> dances, such as those of the Santal and Toda people, the latter, for example, in honour of the god Ön who
brought buffalo to earth.
Among 20th-century directions is the <color=#3366CC>modern dance</color> of <color=#3366CC>Uday Shankar</color> in which classical styles were employed but not
adhered to rigidly. Examples are dance-dramas based on the ancient Indian animal fables, <color=#3366CC>Panchatantra</color>, and Nehru's
mid-century meditation on Indian history, The Discovery of India. Dance has been an essential aspect of Indian films
from the first talkies of the 1930s. The individual and group dances of <color=#3366CC>Bollywood</color>, for example, show a broad range of
influences, including classical, local, and Western popular dance. Towards the end of the 20th century, innovations in
British South Asian music and dance, such as Post-Bhangra, fed back into dance in India.
Clothing
From ancient times until the advent of the modern, the most widely worn traditional dress in India was draped. For
women it took the form of a <color=#3366CC>sari</color>, a single piece of cloth many yards long. The sari was traditionally wrapped around the
lower body and the shoulder. In its modern form, it is combined with an underskirt, or Indian <color=#3366CC>petticoat</color>, and tucked in
along the waist band for more secure fastening. It is also commonly worn with an Indian <color=#3366CC>blouse</color>, or choli, which serves
as the primary upper-body garment, the sari's end—passing over the shoulder—covering the midriff and obscuring the
upper body's contours. For men, a similar but shorter length of cloth, the dhoti, has served as a lower-body garment.
The use of stitched clothes became widespread after Muslim rule was established by the <color=#3366CC>Delhi Sultanate</color> (c. 1300 CE)
and continued by the <color=#3366CC>Mughal Empire</color> (c. 1525 CE). Among the garments introduced during this time and still commonly
worn are: the shalwars and <color=#3366CC>pyjamas</color>, both styles of trousers, and the tunics kurta and kameez. Shalwars are atypically
wide at the waist but narrow to a cuffed bottom. They are held up by a drawstring, which causes them to become
pleated around the waist. When the pants are cut quite narrow, on the bias, they are called churidars. The kameez is a
long shirt or tunic. Its side seams left open below the waistline. The kurta is traditionally collarless and made of cotton
or silk; it is worn plain or with embroidered decoration, such as chikankari; and typically falls to either just above or just
below the wearer's knees.
In the last 50 years, fashion has changed a great deal in India. Increasingly, in urban northern India, the sari is no
longer the apparel of everyday wear, though they remain popular on formal occasions. The traditional shalwar kameez
is rarely worn by younger urban women, who favour churidars or jeans. In office settings, ubiquitous air conditioning
allows men to wear sports jackets year-round. For weddings and formal occasions, men in the middle and upper
classes often wear bandhgala, or short Nehru jackets, with pants, with the groom and his groomsmen sporting
sherwanis and churidars.
Cuisine
The foundation of a typical Indian meal is a cereal cooked plainly and complemented with savoury dishes. The cooked
cereal could be steamed rice; <color=#3366CC>chapati</color>, a thin unleavened bread; idli, a steamed breakfast cake; or <color=#3366CC>dosa</color>, a griddled
pancake. The savoury dishes might include <color=#3366CC>lentils</color>, <color=#3366CC>pulses</color>, vegetables, meat, poultry and fish commonly spiced with

<color=#3366CC>ginger</color> and <color=#3366CC>garlic</color>, but also <color=#3366CC>coriander</color>, <color=#3366CC>cumin</color>, <color=#3366CC>turmeric</color>, <color=#3366CC>cinnamon</color>, <color=#3366CC>cardamom</color> and others. In some instances, the
ingredients may be mixed during the cooking process. India has distinctive vegetarian cuisines, each a feature of the
geographical and cultural histories of its adherents. About 20% to 39% of India's population consists of vegetarians.
Although meat is eaten widely, the proportional consumption of meat is low.
The most significant import of cooking techniques into India during the last millennium occurred during the <color=#3366CC>Mughal</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>, spreading into northern India from regions to its northwest, along with dishes such as <color=#3366CC>pilaf</color>. Onions, garlic,
almonds, and spices were added to the simple yogurt marinade of Persia. Rice was partially cooked and layered
alternately with sauteed meat, the pot sealed tightly, and slow cooked according to another Persian cooking technique,
to produce <color=#3366CC>biryani</color>, a feature of festive dining in many parts of India.
The diversity of Indian food served worldwide has been partially concealed by the dominance of Punjabi cuisine. The
popularity of tandoori chicken—cooked in a tandoor oven, which had traditionally been used for baking bread in the
rural Punjab and the Delhi region, especially among Muslims, but which is originally from <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>—dates to the
1950s, and was caused in large part by an entrepreneurial response among people from the Punjab who had been
displaced by the 1947 partition.
Sports
Sport in modern India is a cultural centre of gravity in whose orbit lie both little-known, indigenous traditions and
commercial sporting spectacles that now have a worldwide reach. Traditional sports such <color=#3366CC>kabaddi</color> and <color=#3366CC>kho-kho</color> have
had a impressive rebirth caused by a large television audience; on the other hand, kushti wrestling in rural
akharas—often regarded by its adherents as not so much a sport as a physical and moral regimen—has continued to
survive away from the glare. When successful, little-known physical cultures or pastimes can be connected vicarously
with <color=#3366CC>cricket</color>, India's most watched sport, and a multi-billion dollar industry. Chess, once a pastime of elderly men in city
parks, has succeeded stunningly among children in southern India, the apex of its rise represented by
eighteen-year-old Gukesh Dommaraju claiming the undisputed World Chess Championship title.
British intervention reshaped India’s athletic landscape. It introduced cricket, <color=#3366CC>football</color> and <color=#3366CC>field hockey</color> and
institutionalised <color=#3366CC>polo</color>—a sport whose history is a case of reverse migration from ancient <color=#3366CC>northeastern India</color> to the West.
Today, at the rural <color=#3366CC>grassroots</color> level, government initiatives like "Khelo India" have democratised athletics for traditionally
overlooked youth. Rural soccer programs have employed teamwork to break down old <color=#3366CC>caste</color> barriers. Increased
government funding for female athletes has brought down other barriers; the much-watched international victories by
boxer Mary Kom and badminton champion P. V. Sindhu have transformed how many in India view women in sports.
<color=#3366CC>India</color> has won eight men's cricket ICC tournament titles: two <color=#3366CC>Cricket World Cups</color>, three T20 World Cups, and three
