In addition to using the approach of soft security for protecting themselves, larger wikis may employ sophisticated
methods, such as bots that automatically identify and revert vandalism. For example, on Wikipedia, the bot ClueBot NG
uses <color=#3366CC>machine learning</color> to identify likely harmful changes, and reverts these changes within minutes or even seconds.
Disagreements between users over the content or appearance of pages may cause edit wars, where competing users
repetitively change a page back to a version that they favor. Some wiki software allows administrators to prevent pages
from being editable until a decision has been made on what version of the page would be most appropriate.
Some wikis may be subject to external structures of governance which address the behavior of persons with access to
the system, for example in academic contexts.
Harmful external links
As most wikis allow the creation of hyperlinks to other sites and services, the addition of malicious hyperlinks, such as
sites infected with <color=#3366CC>malware</color>, can also be a problem. For example, in 2006 a German Wikipedia article about the Blaster
Worm was edited to include a hyperlink to a malicious website, and users of vulnerable Microsoft Windows systems
who followed the link had their systems infected with the worm. Some wiki engines offer a blacklist feature which
prevents users from adding hyperlinks to specific sites that have been placed on the list by the wiki's administrators.
Communities
Applications
The English Wikipedia has the largest user base among wikis on the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color> and ranks in the top 10 among
all Web sites in terms of traffic. Other large wikis include the WikiWikiWeb, Memory Alpha, Wikivoyage, and previously
Susning.nu, a Swedish-language knowledge base. Medical and health-related wiki examples include Ganfyd, an online
collaborative medical reference that is edited by medical professionals and invited non-medical experts. Many wiki
communities are private, particularly within enterprises. They are often used as internal documentation for in-house
systems and applications. Some companies use wikis to allow customers to help produce software documentation. A
study of corporate wiki users found that they could be divided into "synthesizers" and "adders" of content. Synthesizers'
frequency of contribution was affected more by their impact on other wiki users, while adders' contribution frequency
was affected more by being able to accomplish their immediate work. From a study of thousands of wiki deployments,
Jonathan Grudin concluded careful stakeholder analysis and education are crucial to successful wiki deployment.
In 2005, the Gartner Group, noting the increasing popularity of wikis, estimated that they would become mainstream
collaboration tools in at least 50% of companies by 2009. Wikis can be used for <color=#3366CC>project management</color>. Wikis have also
been used in the academic community for sharing and dissemination of information across institutional and
international boundaries. In those settings, they have been found useful for collaboration on grant writing, strategic
planning, departmental documentation, and committee work. In the mid-2000s, the increasing trend among industries
toward collaboration placed a heavier impetus upon educators to make students proficient in collaborative work,
inspiring even greater interest in wikis being used in the classroom.
Wikis have found some use within the legal profession and within the government. Examples include the <color=#3366CC>Central</color>
<color=#3366CC>Intelligence Agency</color>'s Intellipedia, designed to share and collect intelligence assessments, DKosopedia, which was
used by the <color=#3366CC>American Civil Liberties Union</color> to assist with review of documents about the internment of detainees in
Guantánamo Bay; and the wiki of the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, used to post court rules
and allow practitioners to comment and ask questions. The United States Patent and Trademark Office operates
Peer-to-Patent, a wiki to allow the public to collaborate on finding prior art relevant to the examination of pending patent
applications. <color=#3366CC>Queens</color>, New York has used a wiki to allow citizens to collaborate on the design and planning of a local
park. Cornell Law School founded a wiki-based legal dictionary called Wex, whose growth has been hampered by
restrictions on who can edit.
In academic contexts, wikis have also been used as project collaboration and research support systems.
City wikis
A city wiki or local wiki is a wiki used as a <color=#3366CC>knowledge base</color> and <color=#3366CC>social network</color> for a specific <color=#3366CC>geographical</color> locale. The
term city wiki is sometimes also used for wikis that cover not just a city, but a small town or an entire region. Such a wiki
contains information about specific instances of things, ideas, people and places. Such highly localized information
might be appropriate for a wiki targeted at local viewers, and could include:
• Details of public establishments such as public houses, bars, accommodation or social centers
• Owner name, opening hours and statistics for a specific shop
• Statistical information about a specific road in a city
• Flavors of ice cream served at a local ice cream parlor
• A biography of a local mayor and other persons
Growth factors
A study of several hundred wikis in 2008 showed that a relatively high number of administrators for a given content size
is likely to reduce growth; access controls restricting editing to registered users tends to reduce growth; a lack of such
access controls tends to fuel new user registration; and that a higher ratio of administrators to regular users has no
significant effect on content or population growth.
Legal environment
Joint authorship of articles, in which different users participate in correcting, editing, and compiling the finished product,
can also cause editors to become tenants in common of the copyright, making it impossible to republish without
permission of all co-owners, some of whose identities may be unknown due to pseudonymous or anonymous editing.
Some copyright issues can be alleviated through the use of an <color=#3366CC>open content</color> license. Version 2 of the GNU Free
Documentation License includes a specific provision for wiki relicensing, and <color=#3366CC>Creative Commons</color> licenses are also
popular. When no license is specified, an implied license to read and add content to a wiki may be deemed to exist on
the grounds of business necessity and the inherent nature of a wiki.
Wikis and their users can be held liable for certain activities that occur on the wiki. If a wiki owner displays indifference
and forgoes controls (such as banning copyright infringers) that they could have exercised to stop copyright
infringement, they may be deemed to have authorized infringement, especially if the wiki is primarily used to infringe
copyrights or obtains a direct financial benefit, such as advertising revenue, from infringing activities. In the United
States, wikis may benefit from Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects sites that engage in
"<color=#3366CC>Good Samaritan</color>" policing of harmful material, with no requirement on the quality or quantity of such self-policing. It has
also been argued that a wiki's enforcement of certain rules, such as anti-bias, verifiability, reliable sourcing, and
no-original-research policies, could pose legal risks. When <color=#3366CC>defamation</color> occurs on a wiki, theoretically, all users of the
wiki can be held liable, because any of them had the ability to remove or amend the defamatory material from the
"publication". It remains to be seen whether wikis will be regarded as more akin to an <color=#3366CC>internet service provider</color>, which is
generally not held liable due to its lack of control over publications' contents, than a publisher. It has been
recommended that trademark owners monitor what information is presented about their trademarks on wikis, since
courts may use such content as evidence pertaining to public perceptions, and they can edit entries to rectify
misinformation.
Conferences
Active conferences and meetings about wiki-related topics include:
• Atlassian Summit, an annual conference for users of Atlassian software, including Confluence.
• OpenSym (called WikiSym until 2014), an <color=#3366CC>academic conference</color> dedicated to research about wikis and open
collaboration.
• SMWCon, a bi-annual conference for users and developers of Semantic MediaWiki.
• TikiFest, a frequently held meeting for users and developers of Tiki Wiki CMS Groupware.
• Wikimania, an annual conference dedicated to the research and practice of Wikimedia Foundation projects like
Wikipedia.
Former wiki-related events include:
• RecentChangesCamp (2006–2012), an unconference on wiki-related topics.
• RegioWikiCamp (2009–2013), a semi-annual unconference on "regiowikis", or wikis on cities and other geographic
areas.
China
China, officially the People's Republic of China (PRC), is a country in <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>. It is divided into 33 province-level
divisions, including two special administrative regions. <color=#3366CC>Beijing</color> is the capital, while <color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color> is the most populous city
by urban area. Its geography features the <color=#3366CC>Central Plain</color>, major rivers such as the <color=#3366CC>Yangtze</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yellow River</color>, deserts,
<color=#3366CC>subtropical</color> and temperate forests, plateaus, and <color=#3366CC>mountain ranges</color> such as the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color>. It is the world's second-most
populous country after <color=#3366CC>India</color>, with a population exceeding 1.4 billion (17% of the world's population). Covering 9.6
e6sqkm, it is the third largest country by area.
Humans first arrived in China during the <color=#3366CC>Paleolithic</color>. During the 2nd millennium BCE, dynastic states emerged. In 221
BCE, China was unified under the <color=#3366CC>Qin</color>, followed by the <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color>, ushering in two millennia of imperial rule across
periods of unity and division. The imperial era saw the expansion of the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color> and the invention of <color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color>,
<color=#3366CC>paper</color>, <color=#3366CC>printing</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>compass</color>. After increased Western political, economic, and philosophical influence, the empire

was succeeded by the <color=#3366CC>Republic of China</color> (ROC) after the <color=#3366CC>1911 Revolution</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Warlord Era</color> and <color=#3366CC>Chinese Civil War</color>
followed, interrupted by the <color=#3366CC>Second Sino-Japanese War</color>, which ended in a Chinese victory. In 1949, the <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>
<color=#3366CC>Communist Party</color> (CCP) proclaimed the PRC and the <color=#3366CC>ROC retreated to Taiwan</color>. Both sides still claim political
legitimacy. CCP attempts to advance <color=#3366CC>communism</color> faltered through <color=#3366CC>famine</color> and political turmoil. The <color=#3366CC>reform and</color>
<color=#3366CC>opening-up</color> that began in 1978 moved China towards a socialist market economy, spurring economic growth.
China is a <color=#3366CC>unitary state</color> with the CCP as its <color=#3366CC>sole ruling party</color>. It is one of the five permanent members of the <color=#3366CC>UN Security</color>
<color=#3366CC>Council</color> and a member of many multilateral organizations. China is the world's <color=#3366CC>largest manufacturer</color> and has the
second-largest economy by nominal GDP. International organizations have criticized China, alleging authoritarianism
and human rights abuses. Possessing <color=#3366CC>a large military</color>, space program, and nuclear stockpile, China has been
described as a <color=#3366CC>superpower</color> due to its influence in geopolitics, science and technology, manufacturing, <color=#3366CC>economics</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>culture</color>.

<color=#3366CC>Chinese art</color> and culture have <color=#3366CC>influenced much of Asia</color>, with <color=#3366CC>a literary tradition</color> dating back millennia to the <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>

<color=#3366CC>classics</color>. China is the birthplace of <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Daoism</color>, which form the traditional three teachings of <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>

<color=#3366CC>philosophy</color> and <color=#3366CC>folk religion</color> alongside <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>. <color=#3366CC>Chinese cuisine</color> is diverse and highly regional, with rice as a staple in
the south and wheat in the north. It has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the <color=#3366CC>Great Wall</color> and <color=#3366CC>Grand Canal</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Han</color>,
speakers of Sinitic languages, are China's dominant ethnicity, although it is home to 55 recognized minorities, including
the Hui, <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tibetans</color>, <color=#3366CC>Uyghurs</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Zhuang</color>.
Etymology
The word "China" has been used in English since the 16th century; however, it was not used by the Chinese

themselves during this period. Its origin has been traced through <color=#3366CC>Portuguese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Malay</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> back to the <color=#3366CC>Sanskrit</color>
word Cīna, used in ancient India. Cīna was first used in early <color=#3366CC>Hindu</color> scriptures dating from the 3rd century BCE to 4th
century CE, including the <color=#3366CC>Mahabharata</color> and the Laws of Manu. In 1655, the missionary Martino Martini suggested that
the word China is derived ultimately from the ancient state of <color=#3366CC>Qin</color>. This remains a common etymology. Another possible
source is the ancient <color=#3366CC>Guizhou</color> polity of Yelang, known as ina in Loloish languages.
The official name of the modern state is the "People's Republic of China" (Chinese: Zhōnghuá Rénmín Gònghéguó).
The shorter form of this name is Chinese: Zhōngguó, from zhōng ('central' or 'middle') and guó ('state'), a term first
used for the demesne of the Western Zhou dynasty. The names of ruling imperial dynasties were typically used to refer
to the state and its territories. In the 1800s, Chinese: Zhongguo was officially adopted as the name of the country by
the <color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color>.
History
Prehistory
Evidence of early humans such as <color=#3366CC>Homo erectus</color> in China dates to the <color=#3366CC>Paleolithic</color>, around 1.7 million years ago, with
unconfirmed sites as old as 2 million years ago. Modern <color=#3366CC>Homo sapiens</color> are attested from around 50,000 years ago.
Following the end of the <color=#3366CC>Last Glacial Period</color>, in about 8,000 BCE, pottery-making <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> cultures emerged. By the
6000s BCE, sedentary agricultural societies had spread across the lower <color=#3366CC>Yellow River</color> basin. These societies became
increasingly complex, urbanized, and stratified, but many experienced a population collapse in the late 2000s BCE for
unclear reasons.
Ancient China
After 2000 BCE, a <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color> culture emerged in the <color=#3366CC>Central Plain</color>, dubbed the Erlitou culture after its main site.
Erlitou has been controversially identified with the <color=#3366CC>Xia</color>, the traditionally-accepted first dynasty, but no written records
exist to confirm this. The <color=#3366CC>Shang dynasty</color> purportedly succeeded the Xia around 1600 BCE, with its early stages
tentatively identified with an expansionist state known archaeologically as the Erligang culture. The historicity of the
Late Shang is attested through divinational writings in the oracle bone script. These are the earliest known form of
writing in China and the ancestor of modern <color=#3366CC>Chinese characters</color>.
The Shang were overthrown by the <color=#3366CC>Zhou</color> c. 1046 BCE. The Zhou ruled over a vast and loose confederation of vassal
states across central China, which was gradually weakened by regional lords. Centralized authority collapsed in 771
BCE, giving way to constant regional warfare. During the Eastern Zhou, the multitude of small polities of the <color=#3366CC>Spring and</color>
<color=#3366CC>Autumn period</color> evolved into seven territorial <color=#3366CC>Warring States</color>. Literary and philosophical developments of this period

include the emergence of various schools of thought, such as <color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Daoism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mohism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Legalism</color>, alongside
<color=#3366CC>Chinese classics</color> like the Confucian <color=#3366CC>Analects</color> and the Daoist <color=#3366CC>Dao De Jing</color>.
Imperial China
Classical period
In the 220s BCE, <color=#3366CC>Qin</color> rapidly conquered the other warring states. In 221, its ruler <color=#3366CC>Qin Shi Huang</color> proclaimed himself the
first emperor (Chinese: Huángdì) and founded the <color=#3366CC>Qin dynasty</color>. He led an <color=#3366CC>autocratic</color> Legalist state organized in a
system of commanderies and counties. The dynasty lasted only fifteen years, falling soon after his death from <color=#3366CC>revolts</color>
<color=#3366CC>and civil war</color>.
After the collapse, the <color=#3366CC>Han dynasty</color> emerged to rule China between 206 BCE and 220 CE. The Han gradually
reinstated centralized control, legitimizing their rule through Confucian scholarship. Military expeditions against the
<color=#3366CC>Xiongnu</color>, a confederation of nomadic <color=#3366CC>steppe</color> tribes, expanded Han influence into parts of <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> and helped to
establish the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color>, allowing for trade connections between China and western Eurasia. Contemporaneously,
merchants established <color=#3366CC>maritime trade routes</color> linking China, <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, and <color=#3366CC>India</color>.
The Han faced widespread uprisings and the emergence of local warlords in the 100s and 200s CE. By 220, the empire
was split into the <color=#3366CC>Three Kingdoms</color>. These were briefly united by the <color=#3366CC>Jin dynasty</color> in 280, which fell into civil war.
Sinicized formerly-nomadic peoples who had settled in Northern China, such as the Xiongnu, rebelled and <color=#3366CC>founded</color>
<color=#3366CC>new dynasties</color>. <color=#3366CC>Various Han Chinese dynasties in Southern China</color> emerged in the 300s. During these conflicts,
<color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color> was introduced to China via the Silk Road.
Mid-imperial period
China was reunited under the <color=#3366CC>Sui dynasty</color> in 589, which constructed the <color=#3366CC>Grand Canal</color> to link Northern and Southern
China. The Sui collapsed in the 610s, and was succeeded by the <color=#3366CC>Tang</color>. The Tang dynasty centralized the state and
dispatched military expeditions to pacify the surrounding regions. It promoted <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, but through expanding
international trade built a heavily cosmopolitan society centered on its capital of <color=#3366CC>Chang'an</color>. It reformed the <color=#3366CC>civil service</color>
<color=#3366CC>examinations</color> and oversaw a flourishing of art, poetry, architecture, and scholarship. The 755–763 <color=#3366CC>An Lushan rebellion</color>
weakened the Tang, which gradually fragmented before collapsing completely in 907, resulting in <color=#3366CC>another period of war</color>
<color=#3366CC>and division</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Song dynasty</color> rose to power in 960. It faced military crises, unable to subdue its Sinicized non-Han neighbors, the
<color=#3366CC>Khitan</color>-led <color=#3366CC>Liao dynasty</color> and the Tangut-led <color=#3366CC>Western Xia</color>. The Song's consistent focus on defense resulted in a heavily
centralized state and military, which made the first military application of <color=#3366CC>gunpowder</color>. Books became widely available by
the proliferation of <color=#3366CC>printing</color> technology, while the elite class of scholar-officials grew increasingly powerful. Production,
population, and trade expanded massively, alongside innovations such as industrial <color=#3366CC>metallurgy</color> and <color=#3366CC>hydraulic</color>
<color=#3366CC>machinery</color>. The Song capital <color=#3366CC>Kaifeng</color> was overrun by the Jurchen-led <color=#3366CC>Jin</color> in 1127, forcing the Song to retreat to
Southern China. During this period, the revivalist philosophical movement of <color=#3366CC>Neo-Confucianism</color> emerged.
Late imperial period
In 1206, <color=#3366CC>Genghis Khan</color> united the nomadic <color=#3366CC>Mongols</color> to the north under the <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color>. Over the following fifty
years, they conquered the Western Xia and the Jin, in addition to <color=#3366CC>their other conquests</color> as far west as Europe. <color=#3366CC>The</color>
<color=#3366CC>empire split</color> into separate khanates, with Mongol leader <color=#3366CC>Kublai Khan</color> establishing the <color=#3366CC>Yuan dynasty</color> and subjugating the
Song in the 1270s. Although Chinese culture remained largely unchanged, the Yuan maintained a Mongol elite culture
and established a complex ethnic and occupational hierarchy. Foreign presence increased as China became more
connected to Eurasian trade routes.
In the 1340s, central China was devastated by disease, famine, and severe flooding along the Yellow River. <color=#3366CC>Various</color>
<color=#3366CC>rebellions erupted</color>, leading to a peasant leader establishing the <color=#3366CC>Ming dynasty</color> in 1368 and declaring himself the

<color=#3366CC>Hongwu Emperor</color>. The Ming later moved their capital from <color=#3366CC>Nanjing</color> to <color=#3366CC>Beijing</color>, with the <color=#3366CC>Forbidden City</color> as the imperial
palace. However, the lower Yangtze remained the wealthiest region. Trade grew, and the <color=#3366CC>European colonization of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Americas</color> brought new crops and a massive influx of silver to China. The population doubled, and a growing publishing
industry began producing works in vernacular Chinese, including the Four Classic Novels.
The Ming state declined, and by the 1600s, became unable to contain peasant rebellions. The <color=#3366CC>Manchus</color> to the north
declared the <color=#3366CC>Qing dynasty</color> in 1636 and <color=#3366CC>conquered the Ming</color>, killing their last claimant emperor in 1662 and conquering
a Ming rump state on Taiwan in 1683. From the late 1600s to the end of the 1700s, the High Qing era saw economic
growth and territorial expansion westward, including the conquest of Tibet and much of <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>. European powers
fought various wars against the Qing dynasty during the 19th century. These began with the United Kingdom's <color=#3366CC>First</color>
<color=#3366CC>Opium War</color> in 1839–1842, which resulted in the first of the "<color=#3366CC>unequal treaties</color>" imposed on the dynasty. These opened
<color=#3366CC>treaty ports</color>, allowed Christian missionary activity, and loosened trade restrictions. China faced an economic crisis and
internal unrest, and uprisings such as the 1850–1864 <color=#3366CC>Taiping Rebellion</color> resulted in the deaths of millions. Reformist
factions of the Qing responded with the <color=#3366CC>Self-Strengthening Movement</color>, seeking to adopt western weapons and
technologies, but this had a limited impact for much of the empire.
The <color=#3366CC>Empire of Japan</color>'s defeat of the Qing in the <color=#3366CC>First Sino-Japanese War</color> (1894–1895) resulted in the loss of Taiwan
and the growth of both reformist and revolutionary political movements. An imperial push for reform in 1898 ended after
an internal coup, while the anti-foreign <color=#3366CC>Boxer Rebellion</color> was defeated by a coalition of foreign powers in 1901. The late
Qing dynasty again advanced reforms, but growing revolutionary and anti-Manchu sentiment culminated in the <color=#3366CC>1911</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>. A coalition of revolutionaries led by <color=#3366CC>Sun Yat-sen</color> overthrew the Qing and declared the <color=#3366CC>Republic of China</color>
(ROC) in 1912.
Republic of China
President <color=#3366CC>Yuan Shikai</color> rose to power in 1912 and crushed his main opposition, the <color=#3366CC>Kuomintang</color>, ruling China as a
dictator until his death in 1916, following an abortive attempt to restore the monarchy. During the <color=#3366CC>Warlord Era</color>, feuding
regional warlords and governors took power across China, while Tibet and <color=#3366CC>Mongolia</color> declared independence. The
nominal republican government had little control outside Beijing. During this period, New Culture intellectuals and
students criticized traditional society. A crackdown on a student protest in 1919 led to the <color=#3366CC>May Fourth Movement</color> and
further agitation by intellectuals for a cultural and political upheaval, with many embracing Western political ideas such
as <color=#3366CC>communism</color>.In the mid-1920s, the Kuomintang allied with the nascent <color=#3366CC>Chinese Communist Party</color> (CCP), and
partially reunified China under <color=#3366CC>Chiang Kai-shek</color>'s leadership. Starting with the <color=#3366CC>Shanghai massacre</color> in 1927, the
Kuomintang violently purged the CCP and gained the allegiance of the northern warlords, establishing a new
government at Nanjing. The CCP was driven into the countryside and repressed, but subsequently <color=#3366CC>regrouped in the</color>
<color=#3366CC>northwest</color>.
Japan <color=#3366CC>occupied Manchuria</color> in 1931, and launched an <color=#3366CC>invasion of the rest of China</color> in 1937. A renewed coalition
between the CCP and Kuomintang fought Japan in what became a theater of <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, as Japanese forces
committed numerous <color=#3366CC>war atrocities</color> against the civilian population and occupied most of China's major cities. After the
<color=#3366CC>surrender of Japan</color> in 1945, China became a founding member of the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> and regained control over
Manchuria and Taiwan. The <color=#3366CC>civil war</color> between the CCP and the Kuomintang resumed the following year.
People's Republic of China
After a string of military victories, CCP chairman <color=#3366CC>Mao Zedong</color> formally proclaimed the People's Republic of China
(PRC) in 1949. The ROC government <color=#3366CC>retreated to Taiwan</color> and continued to claim legitimacy. The following year, the
PRC <color=#3366CC>occupied and annexed Tibet</color>. The PRC, which the CCP described as a "people's democratic dictatorship",
enacted many reforms: it restructured the economy under state control, promoted literacy and gender equality, and
expanded heavy industry. The <color=#3366CC>Land Reform Movement</color>, in which the state encouraged and organized peasant violence
against landlords, leading to the death of upwards of a million people, had begun in northern China during the civil war
and extended to most of the rest of China between 1950 and 1952. It distributed landlord land to the peasants as
private property, but it was soon followed by collectivization of the land. In 1958, Mao launched the <color=#3366CC>Great Leap</color>
<color=#3366CC>Forward</color>, a mass industrialization project which resulted in the <color=#3366CC>Great Chinese Famine</color> and millions of deaths. As the
<color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> deepened, China <color=#3366CC>grew politically isolated from its former ally</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>, as well as the Western Bloc.
It detonated its first atomic bomb in 1964. Attempting to reassert control over the CCP after the Great Leap, Mao and
his allies launched the <color=#3366CC>Cultural Revolution</color> in 1966, sparking a decade of political violence, crackdowns on perceived
counterrevolutionaries, and social upheaval that lasted until Mao's death in 1976. <color=#3366CC>Deng Xiaoping</color> served as paramount
leader from 1978 to 1989. The <color=#3366CC>reform and opening-up</color> policies of the 1980s and 1990s saw economic liberalization
towards a socialist market economy, rapid economic growth, and improved relations with the West. Political dissent
culminated in crackdowns, such as in the <color=#3366CC>1989 Tiananmen Square massacre</color>. China shifted away from an agricultural
economy and rapidly urbanized, although this led to stark economic inequality between urban and rural areas, as well
as environmental deterioration. Since the 1990s, market forces have become China's main economic driver. Under the
general secretaryship of Xi Jinping since 2012, he has launched a far-reaching <color=#3366CC>anti-corruption campaign</color>, expanded
Chinese economic influence through the <color=#3366CC>Belt and Road Initiative</color>, and abolished <color=#3366CC>term limits</color> for himself as state
president.
Geography
China's geography is highly varied, featuring a <color=#3366CC>dry and mountainous west</color>, alongside both mountains and wide river
valleys in the east. Chinese civilization was traditionally centered in the lowlands around China's two longest rivers: the
<color=#3366CC>Yangtze</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Yellow River</color>, both originating on the <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Plateau</color>. This temperate region is bordered by forest and
<color=#3366CC>steppe</color> to the north, as well as the mountainous and subtropical south. China's shoreline spans the <color=#3366CC>Bohai Sea</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yellow</color>

<color=#3366CC>Sea</color>, <color=#3366CC>East China Sea</color>, and <color=#3366CC>South China Sea</color>, all part of the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ocean</color>. Its largest island is Taiwan, and the largest
governed by the PRC is <color=#3366CC>Hainan</color>. <color=#3366CC>Poyang Lake</color> is the largest of the country's many freshwater lakes.

Large mountain ranges in the west, including the <color=#3366CC>Himalayas</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tian Shan</color>, separate China from <color=#3366CC>South</color> and <color=#3366CC>Central</color>
<color=#3366CC>Asia</color>. China features both the <color=#3366CC>Turpan Depression</color>, among the deepest points on land, and the high Tibetan Plateau.
The world's highest point, <color=#3366CC>Mount Everest</color> (8,848 m above <color=#3366CC>sea level</color>), lies on the border with <color=#3366CC>Nepal</color>. China has a wide
variety of ore and mineral resources.
China's climate is dominated by <color=#3366CC>dry seasons</color> and wet <color=#3366CC>monsoons</color>, which lead to pronounced seasonal temperature
differences. In the winter, northern winds coming from high-latitude areas are cold and dry; in summer, southern winds
from coastal areas at lower latitudes are warm and moist. The northwestern deserts receive as little as 50 mm of rainfall
annually, while much of southern China exceeds 1000 mm. Eastern China is well-suited for agriculture, with two or
three harvests per year. The south is dominated by <color=#3366CC>rice</color> farming, while the north grows crops such as <color=#3366CC>wheat</color> and <color=#3366CC>maize</color>.
China frequently faces natural disasters. Its adjacency to both the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Ring of Fire</color> and the Alpide belt (tectonic
belts) results in frequent earthquakes, the cause of the majority of China's natural disaster deaths. Severe quakes such
as the <color=#3366CC>1976 Tangshan earthquake</color> cause hundreds of thousands of deaths. Rainstorms and flooding are common
hazards, with the Yellow River's perennial floods devastating the surrounding plains throughout recorded history.
<color=#3366CC>Typhoons</color> frequently impact southeastern China.
Environment
China is one of 17 megadiverse countries, containing a wide variety of forests, <color=#3366CC>shrublands</color>, wetlands, <color=#3366CC>steppes</color>, and
deserts, which host (as of 2018) 92,300 known species of plants, animals, and fungi. According to government surveys,
China's forest coverage grew from 10% of the overall territory in 1949 to 25% in 2024. The far north contains <color=#3366CC>taiga</color>,
which transitions into deciduous forest to the south. South of the Yangtze, mixed conifer and deciduous forest is
common, with tropical and subtropical forests farther south.
In the 21st century, China has suffered from environmental deterioration and pollution due to rapid development,
alongside the broader effects of <color=#3366CC>climate change</color>. About 11% of its plant species and 21% of its <color=#3366CC>vertebrate</color> species are
threatened or endangered due to <color=#3366CC>habitat loss</color>, pollution, and <color=#3366CC>poaching</color>. "Flagship" endangered species such as the
<color=#3366CC>giant panda</color> and <color=#3366CC>tiger</color> have received additional funding and protection.
Although China has the world's highest CO2 emissions, it only emits 8 tons of CO2 per capita as of 2020, significantly
lower than many developed countries. Total greenhouse gas emissions by China are the world's largest. China has
prioritized reducing pollution, announcing its aims to reach its peak emissions levels before 2030, and achieve carbon
neutrality by 2060. Water quality in China has been impacted by rapid development and high levels of <color=#3366CC>agricultural</color>
<color=#3366CC>runoff</color> and <color=#3366CC>heavy metal pollution</color>.
China is the world's leading investor in <color=#3366CC>renewable energy</color> and its commercialization, investing in 2022 alone.
Traditionally reliant on non-renewable energy sources such as coal, China's adoption of renewable energy has
increased significantly in recent years. In 2025, 54.4% of China's electricity came from coal, while 41.6% came from
clean energy. Despite its emphasis on renewables, China remains dependent on global oil markets.
Political geography
China is the second-largest country by land area after <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, and the third or fourth largest by total area. Total area
figures range from 9572900 km2 to 9596961 km2. China borders 14 nations, with a combined land border length of
22117 km. Its coastline spans approximately 14500 km.
The PRC has engaged in 23 border disputes since 1949, of which six remain unsettled. It actively disputes several
portions of its Himalayan border with India, including the Aksai Chin in <color=#3366CC>Kashmir</color> and a region administered by India as
<color=#3366CC>Arunachal Pradesh</color>, which led to military skirmishes in 2020. It maintains maritime disputes with Japan over the
Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands and with various countries over a group of South China Sea Islands within the "Nine-dash
line", including the <color=#3366CC>Spratlys</color> and <color=#3366CC>Paracels</color>. This has led to skirmishes with Vietnam and the <color=#3366CC>Philippines</color>.
Both the PRC and the ROC on Taiwan claim legitimacy as the government of China, leading to cross-strait tensions.
Taiwan is a de jure province of the PRC, with the ROC-controlled islands of <color=#3366CC>Kinmen</color> and <color=#3366CC>Matsu</color> as a part of <color=#3366CC>Fujian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Province</color>.
Politics
China is a <color=#3366CC>unitary state</color> under the absolute leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. Since the 1980s, the CCP has
called its guiding theories and policies <color=#3366CC>socialism with Chinese characteristics</color>, which it considers an adapted form of
<color=#3366CC>Marxism–Leninism</color> that emphasizes a market economy as the primary stage of socialism. China describes itself as a
socialist state, and a people's democratic dictatorship. Many academic sources describe it as an <color=#3366CC>authoritarian</color> state,
although others dispute this label.
The <color=#3366CC>National People's Congress</color> (NPC) holds the unified powers of the state and oversight over all state organs, with its
Standing Committee elected to meet between the annual NPC meetings. NPC elections are indirect and the CCP
controls nominations. The NPC elects the president, vice president, military chairman, and chief justice, and approves
the president's nomination for premier (the head of government). In practice, the CCP leadership chooses candidates
for these posts. The premier heads the State Council, which includes 26 ministers, such as the heads of ministries and
commissions. The Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference is an advisory body that formally leads the
CCP's united front system, which aims to gain support from non-CCP intellectuals, eight minor parties, and people's
organizations.
<color=#3366CC>China's current constitution</color> dates to 1982, succeeding two earlier constitutions. Chinese governance is characterized
by a high degree of political centralization but significant economic decentralization. Policy instruments and processes
are often tested locally before being adopted more widely. Surveys have generally shown that the Chinese public has a
high level of support for the government.
Chinese Communist Party
The CCP is the founding and <color=#3366CC>sole ruling party</color> of China, organized along <color=#3366CC>Leninist</color> principles as a vanguard party. With
about 98 million members, it is among the world's largest political parties, as well as the longest-ruling. The party's
highest body is its National Congress, which mainly consists of members elected by party membership and meets
every five years. The National Congress elects the Central Committee, which convenes yearly as the highest party
organ between congresses. The Central Committee ostensibly elects the party's top leadership, the Politburo, Politburo
Standing Committee (PSC) and the general secretary, its top leader. In practice, the committee typically approves a
slate of candidates created by existing party leadership.
The Politburo usually gathers once a month, while the smaller PSC is thought to meet weekly. The current general
secretary is <color=#3366CC>Xi Jinping</color>, who took office on 15 November 2012. Xi concurrently serves as president and the chair of the
Central Military Commission (CMC); as such, he is referred to informally as the paramount leader of China. The
National Congress also elects the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, the party's main disciplinary and
anti-corruption organ.
As the CCP is closely intertwined with the government, disputes within the party represent the main form of political
contention in China. The CCP controls government appointments, with most senior officials being CCP members. The
appointments of CCP cadres and the leadership of major state-owned enterprises and institutions are managed by the
party's Organization Department. The Leninist principle of <color=#3366CC>democratic centralism</color> mandates that party decisions are
binding on all members.
Administrative divisions
China is constitutionally a <color=#3366CC>unitary state</color> divided into 23 provinces, five autonomous regions (each with a designated
minority group), four direct-administered municipalities, as well as the autonomous special administrative regions
(SARs) of Hong Kong and Macau. Provinces and their equivalents are divided into prefectures and prefecture-level
cities. These are divided into counties, county-level cities, and districts. Under these, townships are the basic form of
local government. Direct elections occur only at the township and county levels and below.
Foreign relations
China is one of five permanent members of the <color=#3366CC>United Nations Security Council</color> and the second largest contributor to
the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color>. China has the largest diplomatic network of any country: It has diplomatic relations with 179 United
Nations member states and embassies in 174. China is a member of the <color=#3366CC>G20</color>, <color=#3366CC>BRICS</color>, East Asia Summit, <color=#3366CC>APEC</color>, and
other intergovernmental organizations.
China is widely described as a <color=#3366CC>superpower</color> due to its influence in geopolitics, technology, manufacturing, economics
and culture. Although China moderated its relations with the West during the <color=#3366CC>reform era</color>, its rise in power has brought
political tensions with many of its neighbors and with the United States, the current dominant superpower. Although
China is among the United States' largest trade partners, their relationship is tempered by <color=#3366CC>a trade war</color> and
disagreements over the political status of Taiwan.
China's foreign policy is based on the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, which include a principle of
non-intervention in other countries' domestic affairs. Per its policy of non-alignment, China has no defense pacts except
for its 1961 treaty with <color=#3366CC>North Korea</color>, although it maintains close relationships with neighbors such as <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> and
Russia. China has invested heavily in <color=#3366CC>developing countries</color> across Asia, <color=#3366CC>Latin America</color>, and Africa, creating a system of
development banks and loans through the <color=#3366CC>Belt and Road Initiative</color>.
Military
The <color=#3366CC>People's Liberation Army</color> (PLA) is the main armed forces of China, under the direct control of the CCP. It consists
of four services: the Ground Force, the Navy, the Air Force, and the Rocket Force, and four arms: the Aerospace
Force, the Cyberspace Force, the Information Support Force, and the Joint Logistics Support Force. It has around 2
million active soldiers, and the world's third largest stockpile of nuclear weapons, and the world's largest navy by ship
count.
The PLA is considered one of the world's most powerful militaries and has rapidly modernized in the recent decades. A
2026 study estimates that its 2025 expenditure was 2.27 trillion yuan (US$336 billion), 12% of global military spending
and 1.7% of China's GDP. The PLA, the People's Armed Police and the Militia are commanded by the Central Military
Commission. Due to the chairman responsibility system, the chairman of the CMC, currently Xi Jinping, is the
commander-in-chief of the PLA.
Law and policing
The Chinese judicial system consists of people's courts at provincial, regional, and local levels, alongside circuit courts
for regional matters and specialized courts to handle professional disputes. The highest legal authority is the <color=#3366CC>Supreme</color>
<color=#3366CC>People's Court</color>. The courts are closely controlled by the CCP, supervised by corresponding people's congresses, and

led by CCP appointees. <color=#3366CC>PRC law</color> derives from a combination of <color=#3366CC>civil law</color>, <color=#3366CC>traditional Chinese law</color>, and <color=#3366CC>socialist law</color>.
China's law enforcement system is managed by the Ministry of Public Security, which oversees public security bureaus
(PSBs) in each province, themselves divided into local levels. Local sub-bureaus and stations handle most routine
policing. The People's Armed Police, a <color=#3366CC>paramilitary</color> force, is administered by the CMC and supports emergency
response measures. The social credit system maintains a network of blacklists to record businesses and individuals
who violate regulations, court orders, or financial agreements. China has periodically mobilized anti-crime campaigns,
using heavy penalties as a form of deterrence. Violent crimes are the highest priority for enforcement, although they
occur at relatively low rates. Capital punishment has declined since the Mao era, but remains common; China has the
most executions per year of any country.
Human rights
Various human rights organizations, United Nations assessments, and foreign governments have accused China of
severe human rights violations. It has been accused of political repression, torture, indefinite detention, restrictions on
free speech and religious practice, excessive use of capital punishment, and the persecution of ethnic
minorities.Although the Chinese constitution protects a wide variety of civil and political rights, these largely lack
enforcement mechanisms. The petitioning system allows citizens to raise complaints of wrongdoing, although the
concerns are often left unaddressed, and some petitioners have faced punitive arrest or incarceration. In the 21st
century, China has participated extensively in the United Nations Human Rights Council, but remains strongly critical of
international scrutiny of its human rights, seeing it as interference in its internal affairs.
In <color=#3366CC>Xinjiang</color>, China has restricted the civil rights of the <color=#3366CC>Uyghurs</color>, who face <color=#3366CC>widespread discrimination</color>, police crackdowns,
and restrictions on Islamic religious practice and the use of the <color=#3366CC>Uyghur language</color>. China interred over a million Uyghurs
in a network of internment camps in the late 2010s. These facilities have evolved into a system of prisons and <color=#3366CC>forced</color>
<color=#3366CC>labor</color>. Several UN OHCHR experts have equated it to "enslavement as a <color=#3366CC>crime against humanity</color>". China has restricted
the civil and political rights of <color=#3366CC>Hong Kong</color> residents. Since the <color=#3366CC>2019–2020 protests</color>, China has cracked down on the
pro-democracy movement in the SAR and removed much of its political autonomy. China has cracked down on political
expression in Tibet and strengthened surveillance since the late 2000s, restricting residents from obtaining passports
and most foreigners from entering the region.
China does not recognize <color=#3366CC>same-sex marriage</color> or same-sex adoption, and regularly censors <color=#3366CC>LGBTQ</color>-related media.
Many Chinese hospitals provide sexual conversion therapy, viewing homosexuality as a mental disorder. LGBTQ rights
advocates are surveilled and criminalized.
Economy
The modern PRC is often described by analysts as an example of <color=#3366CC>state capitalism</color> or party-state capitalism, with both
market forces and the state playing a major role in the economy. Various state organs manage the economy according
to the State Council's five-year plans. China describes its economic system as a socialist market economy, in which the
market plays a decisive role in resource allocation under the control of a socialist state. The Chinese economy has
expanded more than 20 times since 2000. It is now the second largest economy by GDP (135 trillion yuan) and the
largest when adjusted for <color=#3366CC>purchasing power parity</color>. China has brought roughly 800 million people out of extreme
poverty, more than any other country in history.
China is the world's leading manufacturing power, accounting for 28% of global manufacturing as of 2024; it is the
largest producer of steel, rare earths, ships, and automobiles, as well as the largest exporter of electronics and textiles.
The private sector constitutes the largest portion of the Chinese economy, with about 30–40% under state ownership.
State-owned companies make less than 10% of exports, but are predominant in industries such as transportation,
utilities, and financial services. Since the 1990s, China has decentralized its economic planning, with about 85% of
government spending delegated to the provincial or local level, and local governments adapting national economic
plans to suit local interests.
China's main <color=#3366CC>stock exchanges</color> are <color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color> and Shenzhen. Its stock market is the second largest, behind the US. The
Chinese banking system makes up a much larger share of the economy than most other countries. Four state-owned
banks hold about 40% of the sector's assets as of 2022. China has struggled to establish its currency, the <color=#3366CC>renminbi</color> (in
units of yuan), as an international <color=#3366CC>reserve currency</color>; as of 2025, it is the seventh largest currency in foreign exchange
reserves.
About a third of China's workforce consists of domestic migrant workers, the floating population. The Chinese: <color=#3366CC>hukou</color>
system restricts citizens' access to services and utilities outside of their registered home, leading to pronounced
inequalities between urban and rural workers. Especially in larger cities, only those with local Chinese: hukou may be
able to buy property, though hukou restrictions have loosened significantly in recent decades.
According to 2026 state data, China's urban unemployment rate was 5.0%. China has a high debt-to-GDP ratio (almost
300% in 2020), with household debt at about 65% of the GDP. China has faced a property sector crisis since 2020. By
the late 2010s, Chinese real estate assets far exceed the combined total of stocks, <color=#3366CC>bonds</color>, and deposits.
Science and technology
As the world's largest economy for much of its history, many inventions and scientific discoveries have been produced
in China, including paper, printing, the compass, and gunpowder. China has pursued rapid technological development
since the reform era. It has made great advances in the fields of <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color>, <color=#3366CC>robotics</color>, and <color=#3366CC>biotechnology</color>, while
the Xi administration has prioritized green technology and reducing Chinese dependence on foreign technology. It has
emphasized <color=#3366CC>technocratic</color> leadership in the 2020s, promoting experts in scientific fields to national leadership positions,
while bringing major private technology firms such as <color=#3366CC>Tencent</color> and <color=#3366CC>Alibaba</color> under state regulation. Geopolitical tensions
have led Europe and the United States to restrict Chinese access to their technology, especially <color=#3366CC>semiconductors</color>, and
launch sanctions targeting the telecommunications and electronics firm <color=#3366CC>Huawei</color>.
Since launching its first satellite in 1970, China has maintained an active space program. After the United States and
the Soviet Union, China became the third country to independently launch an orbital satellite, and in 2003 became the
third to bring astronauts into orbit. The <color=#3366CC>Chinese Lunar Exploration Program</color> has sent multiple robotic landers to the
Moon, the Planetary Exploration of China program has sent a lander and rover to <color=#3366CC>Mars</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Tiangong space station</color>
has hosted crewed operations in <color=#3366CC>Low Earth orbit</color> since 2021.
Infrastructure and transportation
Since the 1990s, automobiles have become a common form of transport in China. According to state data, the Chinese
highway network exceeded 6,000,000 km by the end of 2021, having grown 30% over the past decade. In addition to
local and provincial routes, this network includes the national highways, which are divided between the ordinary
highways (of various classes) and the national expressway system. China has the largest highway and rail systems in
the world by capacity, along with the second longest rail network at roughly 165000 km. According to 2022 state data,
over 95% of cities exceeding one million residents have access to high-speed rail. Out of the 50 busiest container
ports, 18 are located in China, including the world's busiest, the <color=#3366CC>Port of Shanghai</color>. China has the largest domestic
aviation market by passenger capacity, and maintains 262 airports as of 2025.
Chinese cities are disparate in their level of infrastructure. Tier-one cities such as Beijing and Shanghai have elaborate
and advanced infrastructure networks, while smaller cities and rural areas often have outdated and underfunded transit
and public utilities. Water resources in China are unevenly distributed. With industrialization and rapid development, the
drier north has faced endemic water shortages. To combat this, the South–North Water Transfer Project pumps water
from the Yangtze basin to supply northern cities.
The <color=#3366CC>State Grid Corporation of China</color>, the world's largest <color=#3366CC>utility company</color>, manages the <color=#3366CC>electrical grid</color> for most of the
country, with the China Southern Power Grid as the electric utility in some southern provinces. Power generation is
primarily managed by five state-owned corporations, alongside local and provincial utilities. Most of China's renewable
energy comes from hydropower. The <color=#3366CC>Three Gorges Dam</color> is the world's largest power station by capacity.
China has the largest number of internet users and websites of any country. According to state data, it has 1.125 billion
internet users as of 2025, about 80% of its population. It has an extensive system of internet censorship. The Great
Firewall, a system of internet controls and regulations, blocks access to many foreign websites. Users can circumvent it
through virtual private networks, but these face occasional crackdowns. The Cyberspace Administration of China is the
national internet regulator and censor. Most telecommunications are operated by state-owned companies.
Demographics
The 2020 Chinese census recorded the population as 1,411,778,724. About 17.95% were 14 years old or younger,
63.35% were between 15 and 59, and 18.7% were over 60. Between 2010 and 2020, the average population growth
rate was 0.53%. Since 2022, deaths have outpaced births. China has one of the lowest total fertility rates (births per
woman) in the world, around 1.0 as of 2025. China has a rapidly aging population: the proportion of Chinese over 65 is
predicted to reach 26% by 2050, which would create a large economic and social burden from increased need for
caretakers and medical assistance.
The National Bureau of Statistics estimated that the population fell 850,000 from 2021 to 2022, the first decline since
1961. In 2025, China recorded 5.6 births per 1000 people, the lowest recorded birthrate since at least 1949. China's
population is concentrated in the eastern half of the country; although 64% of China's territory is west of the
Heihe–Tengchong Line, as of 2020 only 6.5% of its population lives west of the line.
Spurred by fears of overpopulation, China maintained a <color=#3366CC>one-child policy</color> from 1979 to 2015, restricting most families to
a single child. The policy was most strictly enforced in urban areas, while families from ethnic minorities and rural
communities were often exempt from one-child limits. A two-child policy was introduced in 2015, and in July 2021,
family size limits as well as penalties for exceeding them were removed. The policy resulted in a skewed sex ratio, as
many families preferred to have sons, who were able to continue the patrilineal line and were perceived as better able
to support the family. Through a combination of infanticide, <color=#3366CC>sex-selective abortion</color>, and unreported female births, there
were 120 boys born for every 100 girls by the late 1990s.
China maintains a restrictive immigration policy, with permanent residence granted to only around 12,000 foreigners as
of 2023, while an additional 845,697 foreign nationals lived in Mainland China as of the 2020 census. The <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>
<color=#3366CC>diaspora</color> is among the largest on earth, comprising about 40 million people, mostly descended from emigrants during
the 19th and early 20th centuries. About two-thirds of this diaspora reside in Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and the
United States.
Cities and urbanization
China has urbanized significantly in recent decades. The percentage of the country's population living in urban areas
increased from 20% in 1980 to over 68% in 2025, according to Chinese government figures, while the United Nations
calculates the 2025 urbanization rate as 83.7%. Cities in China often include smaller towns and rural areas under their

jurisdiction. <color=#3366CC>Shanghai</color> is its most populous city by urban area. Two <color=#3366CC>urban agglomerations</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Pearl Delta</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yangtze</color>
<color=#3366CC>Delta</color>, contain many of the largest cities and tens of millions of people.
The figures below are from the 2020 census and are only estimates of the urban populations within administrative city
limits; a different ranking exists for total municipal populations. The large floating population of migrant workers make
conducting censuses in urban areas difficult.
Languages and ethnic groups
China legally recognizes 56 distinct ethnic groups. The largest of these are the <color=#3366CC>Han Chinese</color>, who constitute more than
91% of the total population. The minority groups are generally found in the western and border regions of China. Social
and wealth inequalities exist between many minority groups and the Han, especially in the rural <color=#3366CC>southwestern areas</color>.
Most Han are speakers of <color=#3366CC>Mandarin Chinese</color>, of which <color=#3366CC>Standard Chinese</color> is a standardized form and the official
language of China. Around 300 million people speak other Chinese languages (often described as —local varieties or
<color=#3366CC>dialects</color>—in Chinese sources). While also written with <color=#3366CC>Chinese characters</color>, these are not highly mutually intelligible with

Mandarin or each other. Major branches of Chinese include Mandarin, <color=#3366CC>Wu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Yue</color> (Cantonese), <color=#3366CC>Min</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hakka</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Xiang</color>; the latter six are mainly spoken in Southern China. Since the 1950s, local dialects have steadily assimilated into
Mandarin or one of the main regional registers.
<color=#3366CC>Simplified Chinese characters</color>, first standardized in the 1950s, are used to write Chinese throughout Mainland China,
while <color=#3366CC>traditional Chinese characters</color> remain in use in the SARs and Taiwan. <color=#3366CC>Hanyu Pinyin</color> is the official <color=#3366CC>romanization</color>
<color=#3366CC>system for Chinese</color> in the PRC.
Other language families are found throughout China. Distantly related to Chinese, Tibeto-Burman languages are found
in the west and southwest. In southwestern China, many Hmong–Mien and <color=#3366CC>Kra–Dai languages</color> are spoken by minority
groups. Offshoots of the <color=#3366CC>Austroasiatic</color> and <color=#3366CC>Austronesian language families</color> are also found in the south in smaller
numbers. In the northwest, <color=#3366CC>Turkic</color> (including <color=#3366CC>Uyghur</color>) and Mongolic languages are found, as well as two <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color>

<color=#3366CC>languages</color> (<color=#3366CC>Russian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tajik</color>). Several <color=#3366CC>Tungusic languages</color> are found in northwestern and northeastern China. Since
the 2010s, the Chinese government has intensified linguistic assimilation policies, generally requiring schools to use
Standard Chinese.
Religion
The Chinese religious tradition is heavily syncretic, incorporating various <color=#3366CC>folk religious practices</color> alongside
<color=#3366CC>Confucianism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Taoism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>. These 'three teachings' were the three main institutionalized schools of Chinese
religion. These exist alongside introduced minority religions such as <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> and <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, as well as various new
religious movements. Statistics on affiliation are difficult to gather due to varying definitions of religion and the diffusive
nature of local traditions. Many people follow religious teachings and practices without considering themselves
adherents. <color=#3366CC>Local deities</color> are commonly worshiped alongside widely known gods, such as <color=#3366CC>Guan Yu</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mazu</color>.
Confucianism is a philosophical and spiritual tradition that originated in the Eastern Zhou, emphasizing the study of the
<color=#3366CC>classics</color> and the relations of the individual, society, and <color=#3366CC>heaven</color>. It has sometimes been identified as a religion,
following western influences. Daoism emphasizes the Chinese: <color=#3366CC>Dao</color> ('way') as the world's origin and fundamental force,
and seeks to harness it through spiritual cultivation. Initially a philosophical movement during the Eastern Zhou, the
religious tradition of Daoism emerged during the 2nd century CE. <color=#3366CC>Mahayana Buddhism</color> was introduced to China during
the Han dynasty and spread rapidly over the following centuries. Although often dismissed by Confucian elites,
Buddhism greatly influenced other Chinese religious and philosophical traditions.
Although China and CCP are legally atheist, freedom of religion is formally guaranteed by the Chinese constitution.
China officially recognizes five religions: Buddhism, Taoism, Islam, Catholicism, and Protestantism. Formal religious
practice is managed by "patriotic associations" for each of the recognized faiths overseen by the CCP's United Front
Work Department. However, the majority of religious activities take place outside of registered organizations. China has
attempted to crack down on some forms of unregistered practice, such as Protestant house churches. Religious
practices among minority groups, such as Islam among the Uyghur and <color=#3366CC>Tibetan Buddhism</color>, have come under state
scrutiny and regulation over fears of separatism.
Education
Following an optional two to three years of preschool, China has nine years of free <color=#3366CC>compulsory education</color>, generally
with six years of elementary school and three years of junior high school. If they pass entrance examinations, students
may then attend a senior high school, choosing between an academic or <color=#3366CC>vocational</color> track. The Chinese: gaokao exams
allow access to <color=#3366CC>undergraduate</color> higher education, with additional examinations required to attend postgraduate
programs. As of 2022, 95% of junior high students continue to high school, while higher education has a 59.6%
enrollment rate.
As of 2022, China had 158 million students enrolled in compulsory school, and 46.5 million enrolled in higher
education. There are over 200,000 elementary and junior high schools, over 22,000 secondary schools, and over 3,000
colleges and universities. Both private and public schools exist at all levels, with 10.6% of elementary and junior high
students attending private schools. China became the world's largest publisher of scientific papers in 2016. <color=#3366CC>Foreign</color>
<color=#3366CC>language</color> programs are mandatory from 3rd grade. Generally focused on English, other languages are increasingly
being taught, especially at the senior high level.
Health
The vast majority of primary health care institutions in China offer both allopathic and <color=#3366CC>traditional Chinese medicine</color>
(TCM). In 2017, there were approximately 9,000 community health centers in urban areas—which oversaw roughly
25,000 health stations—and 37,000 township health centers in rural areas. There were about 639,000 village clinics,
which operate as independent, for-profit enterprises subsidized by the state.
The National Health Commission, together with its local counterparts, oversees health policy. After the beginning of
reform and opening-up in 1978, Chinese public health improved rapidly from better nutrition, although many free health
services provided in the countryside disappeared. Healthcare in China became mostly privatized and experienced a
significant quality increase. China is a major producer and exporter of active pharmaceutical ingredients.
According to 2025 state data, the <color=#3366CC>life expectancy</color> at birth exceeds 79 years, and the <color=#3366CC>infant mortality rate</color> is 4 per 1,000.
Rates of <color=#3366CC>stunted growth</color> declined from 33.1% in 1990 to 4.5% in 2024. Mental health services are underfunded and
unevenly distributed. The <color=#3366CC>COVID-19 pandemic</color> was first identified in <color=#3366CC>Wuhan</color>. China maintained a zero-COVID policy,
using lockdowns, <color=#3366CC>quarantines</color>, and contact tracing to curb its transmission, until protests in November–December 2022.
Culture
Beginning in the Qin and Han dynasties and continuing over the following millennia, <color=#3366CC>an area of Chinese cultural</color>
<color=#3366CC>influence</color> grew to encompass much of East Asia. Japan, Korea, and Vietnam adopted various political, philosophical,
religious, and aesthetic concepts from China, facilitated by their adoption of <color=#3366CC>Chinese characters</color> and participation in the
<color=#3366CC>tributary system</color>. China has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the <color=#3366CC>Great Wall</color> and Grand Canal, the second most of
any country (behind <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>).
Chinese culture has historically emphasized family connections, with filial piety and the <color=#3366CC>veneration of ancestors</color> seen as
vital duties under Confucian ethics. Prior to the 20th century, family relations were highly <color=#3366CC>patriarchal</color>, and <color=#3366CC>arranged</color>
<color=#3366CC>marriages</color> were commonplace. The CCP pushed for gender equality after coming to power, establishing the All-China
Women's Federation to manage women's issues. However, many patriarchal gender norms remain prevalent, and
women face lower employment rates and occupational gender segregation.
Prior to the adoption of the <color=#3366CC>Gregorian calendar</color> in 1912, China traditionally used a 12-month <color=#3366CC>lunisolar calendar</color>. The
60-part sexagenary cycle was often used to enumerate days as well as years, alongside the twelve-year <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>
<color=#3366CC>zodiac</color>. Major holidays and festivals in China include the <color=#3366CC>Chinese New Year</color> (or Spring Festival), the <color=#3366CC>Qingming Festival</color>,
the <color=#3366CC>Mid-Autumn Festival</color>, and National Day.
Art
Traditional Chinese art makes use of a wide array of common motifs, metaphors, and symbols, often using nature as
allegory. During the imperial period, skill in art was a marker of refinement and high social status. Renowned art pieces
often bear inscriptions and seals from their previous owners, allowing for the tracing of provenance over long periods of
time.
Chinese paintings are traditionally made with ink brushes on paper or <color=#3366CC>silk</color>. Horizontal handscrolls and vertical hanging
scrolls are common formats, alongside <color=#3366CC>wall paintings</color>, folding screens and hand fans. <color=#3366CC>Calligraphy</color>, emerging during the
3rd and 4th centuries CE, was traditionally regarded in China as the most prestigious form of art, and remains among
the most widely practiced. Western painting styles gained popularity during the early 20th century, while the Mao
government promoted art as a means to embody socialist ideals. The 21st century has seen a boom in the international
influence of Chinese <color=#3366CC>contemporary art</color>.
Pottery and metal crafts in China date to ancient times. <color=#3366CC>Porcelain</color>, also known as china, became a common form of
ceramic during the 7th century. By the 14th century, it became popular to decorate porcelain vessels with elaborate
blue and white patterns, which became the most popular form of Chinese ceramics. <color=#3366CC>Jade</color> crafts and lacquerware have
been common decorative mediums since antiquity.
Architecture
Wood is the most commonly used material in traditional <color=#3366CC>Chinese architecture</color>. Roofs of important buildings, generally
ceramic tile, are often ornate and hipped. Traditional buildings are often arranged around <color=#3366CC>cardinal directions</color>, with
grandeur expressed through large complexes, often featuring <color=#3366CC>courtyards</color> and large gates. The spiritual concept of <color=#3366CC>feng</color>
<color=#3366CC>shui</color> influences the layout of houses and settlements, oriented around the flow of <color=#3366CC>qi</color>, vital energy.
<color=#3366CC>Pagodas</color>, multi-story religious towers far taller than other forms of traditional architecture, were introduced to China
alongside Buddhism, and comprise many of China's oldest buildings. Western-style architecture was introduced during
the 1800s, while domestic architects began to implement Western design principles in the 1900s. The reform era has
seen a boom in contemporary skyscrapers and offices, which have largely supplanted traditional architecture.
Performing arts
The <color=#3366CC>music of China</color> is highly diverse and regional. Traditional Chinese music uses a wide variety of instruments,
including the Chinese: dizi (a flute), Chinese: erhu (a bowed string instrument), Chinese: <color=#3366CC>guqin</color> (a plucked string
instrument), Chinese: <color=#3366CC>guzheng</color> (a plucked <color=#3366CC>zither</color>), Chinese: pipa (a <color=#3366CC>lute</color>), Chinese: sheng (a mouth organ), Chinese:
suona (a wind instrument), and various types of bells and drums. Western-style music spread during the early 20th
century, leading the Chinese orchestra to develop as a fusion of Western orchestral music with Chinese instruments.
Western <color=#3366CC>classical music</color> remains highly prestigious. Inspired by Western <color=#3366CC>jazz</color> and boosted by the introduction of
recording studios, <color=#3366CC>Mandarin pop music</color> emerged in Shanghai in the 1920s, while the folk rock-inspired <color=#3366CC>Cantopop</color>
became popular around Hong Kong during the 1970s. After reform and opening-up, various forms of pop and rock
music reached widespread popularity.
<color=#3366CC>Chinese opera</color> emerged from shuochang, folk narrative singing traditions. Influenced by various regional traditions and
Chinese: kunqu, a genre popular during the Ming dynasty, <color=#3366CC>Peking opera</color> reached national popularity during the Qing
dynasty, while various local and regional forms of opera emerged across the country. Maoist China promoted
<color=#3366CC>revolutionary opera</color> and communist-oriented folk music.
By the Han period, Chinese dance was a frequent subject of art and poetry, as well as an element of religious rites.
Dancers often performed for the imperial courts, while Chinese opera dances led to increasing numbers of dance
troupes across all levels of society during the Qing. Western dances gained popularity in the early 20th century, while
the CCP promoted <color=#3366CC>folk dances</color> such as yangge.
Cuisine
Chinese meals generally incorporate a grain (Chinese: fan) alongside meat or vegetable-based dishes (Chinese: cai).

Flour—as steamed buns, <color=#3366CC>dumplings</color>, pancakes, or <color=#3366CC>noodles</color>—is the primary grain in the north, alongside <color=#3366CC>maize</color>, <color=#3366CC>millet</color>,

<color=#3366CC>rice</color>, and in some regions, <color=#3366CC>sorghum</color>. Rice—steamed or in the form of <color=#3366CC>congee</color>, <color=#3366CC>rice noodles</color> or <color=#3366CC>rice cakes</color>—dominates in
the south. Although Chinese cuisine is highly diverse and regional, pork, chicken, fish, and duck are the most common

meats. Soybeans are a common staple nationally made into products such as <color=#3366CC>tofu</color> and <color=#3366CC>soy sauce</color>. <color=#3366CC>Stir frying</color> in <color=#3366CC>woks</color> is
the most common cooking method, alongside deep-frying, steaming, and <color=#3366CC>hot pot</color>, where dishes are cooked in
simmering broth at the table.
People in China generally eat three meals a day, often with a simple breakfast and a more elaborate dinner. <color=#3366CC>Chopsticks</color>
are the main eating utensil. Dishes are usually served to be shared among multiple people, rather than served in
individual portions. Hot tea almost always accompanies meals across the country, in lieu of water. Alcohol such as <color=#3366CC>rice</color>
<color=#3366CC>wines</color> and the distilled liquor baijiu are commonly served with meals. Chinese cuisine was traditionally divided into four
great traditions: Lu (Shandong), Yang (Jiangsu), <color=#3366CC>Chuan</color> (Sichuan), and <color=#3366CC>Yue</color> (Guangdong). Chinese Buddhists have
developed a unique cuisine that avoids meat, while Chinese Islamic cuisine excludes pork and alcohol.
Fashion
Various forms of robe served as the main form of clothing for men and women throughout Chinese history, adapting
over the centuries. Silk, hemp, and later cotton were the main textiles. Both men and women generally bound their hair
with caps or pins, except during periods where foreign hairstyles were enforced by the elite.
Chinese fashions changed greatly during the 20th century, as traditional designs largely gave way to western clothing.
The Chinese: qipao became a popular form of women's dress during the early 20th century, but are today rare outside
of formal occasions. After a focus on simple, practical clothing during the Mao era, the reform era saw the emergence
of a Western-style fashion industry. In the 21st century, the Hanfu movement has sought to promote a reconstructed
form of traditional Chinese clothing.
Literature
China has among the longest continuous literary traditions in the world. Late Shang-era oracle bone inscriptions are the
oldest known form of Chinese writing, while the oldest surviving literary works—such as the <color=#3366CC>Book of Documents</color>—date
to the early Zhou. The Chinese literary canon was historically centered on the <color=#3366CC>Five Classics</color> (ancient transmitted texts)
and the <color=#3366CC>Four Books</color> (central Confucian texts). The literati regarded literature as primarily didactic, with fiction seen as
useless and potentially corruptive. However, poetry was viewed highly for its ability to convey the nature of reality. The
poetry of the Tang era was particularly prized in later dynasties.
<color=#3366CC>Classical Chinese</color> was the standard literary register until the early 20th century, when it was overtaken by written
vernacular Chinese. Before this, fiction was generally written in vernacular Chinese, with formal works generally in
Classical Chinese. Popular vernacular literature spread with the introduction of printing, resulting in works such as the
Four Classic Novels of the Ming and Qing periods.
Modern Chinese literature has been heavily influenced by the political upheavals of the 19th and 20th centuries,
seeking to explain the political climate or imagine its future. New Culture writers such as <color=#3366CC>Lu Xun</color> promoted the
importance of fiction and vernacular Chinese, experimenting with new modernist forms, while writers of the Reform era
sought to explain the trauma of the Mao era.
Media
China's largest media company is <color=#3366CC>China Central Television</color>, which competes with various provincial television
networks. China is the largest online video market, with its major streaming platforms including iQIYI, Youku, and Sohu.
As of 2025, the <color=#3366CC>Chinese film industry</color> is the second largest by global box office earnings (behind the United States),
although 98% of earnings are domestic. China limits the number of foreign films that can be shown domestically.
According to state sources, it has over 90,000 cinema screens as of 2025, more than any other country.
As of 2023, China has over 2,600 radio stations, all state-owned, and over 1,900 newspapers. Cities generally have a
newspaper published by the local government and another by the local CCP branch. Journalism is tightly controlled
and monitored by the CCP, with content critical of the government censored. Foreign Chinese-language news outlets
are blocked, while English-language outlets are occasionally available but often censored. Prominent newspapers in
China include the <color=#3366CC>People's Daily</color>, <color=#3366CC>Global Times</color>, China Daily, and Reference News. The most popular social media
platform is <color=#3366CC>WeChat</color>. Other major platforms include the microblogging service <color=#3366CC>Weibo</color>, the news and content aggregator
Toutiao, the video-sharing platform Xigua Video, and the short-form video platform <color=#3366CC>Douyin</color>, available internationally as
<color=#3366CC>TikTok</color>.
Sport and games
Traditional sports such as <color=#3366CC>martial arts</color> and <color=#3366CC>dragon boat racing</color> have been practiced in China for over a millennium. The
ball game Chinese: <color=#3366CC>cuju</color> predates the Qin dynasty and remained popular for millennia, declining during the late <color=#3366CC>Qing</color>
<color=#3366CC>dynasty</color>. Chuiwan (similar to modern <color=#3366CC>golf</color>) and <color=#3366CC>polo</color> were popular sports among elites throughout portions of the
imperial period, while commoners played regional ball games. Modern sporting was introduced to China from the West
during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. China first participated in the <color=#3366CC>Olympic Games</color> in 1932. Although
<color=#3366CC>association football</color> draws large audiences, the men's national team has only qualified once for the <color=#3366CC>FIFA World Cup</color>;
the country hosted the <color=#3366CC>FIFA Women's World Cup</color> twice and the women's team finished as runners-up once.
China began to invest heavily in elite sports during the 1990s, and in 2008 Beijing hosted the Summer Olympics. Elite
sports in China are managed by the General Administration of Sport, which oversees management centers for various
sports, as well as provincial sports committees and teams. The vast majority of sports funding, especially for elite
sports, comes from the government. China hosted the Winter Olympics in 2022, and the <color=#3366CC>Asian Games</color> in 1990, 2010,
and 2022. China is dominant among international competition in table tennis (often dubbed China's national sport),
<color=#3366CC>badminton</color>, <color=#3366CC>diving</color>, and <color=#3366CC>weightlifting</color>, and is among the top global competitors in <color=#3366CC>snooker</color>.
Various card, dice, and board games gained popularity in imperial China, most notably Chinese: <color=#3366CC>weiqi</color> (also known as
